sub: 1750–1827 · The sonata principle: drama made of keys
k: classical 1750–1827 · the sonata principle: drama made of keys the continuo falls away and melody is set over a lighter accompaniment. music is now built in balanced phrases and organised by the tension between two keys: the sonata principle, which shapes symphonies, quartets and concertos. haydn invents its procedures, mozart makes them sing, beethoven makes them fight. period sentence sonata form development string quartet cadenza fortepiano

title: Romanticism
sub: 1815–1890 · The song, the self and the swelling orchestra
k: romanticism 1815–1890 · the song, the self and the swelling orchestra the composer becomes a hero and the listener a confidant. harmony grows chromatic, forms stretch to hold a programme or a poem, the piano becomes an orchestra under ten fingers, and national idioms — polish, bohemian, russian — enter the concert hall. from schubert’s songs to wagner’s music drama. chromatic mediant character piece song cycle thematic transformation leitmotif cyclic form programme music rubato

title: Fin de siècle
sub: 1880–1918 · The late-Romantic sunset, at its most extravagant
k: fin de siecle 1880–1918 · the late-romantic sunset, at its most extravagant orchestras of a hundred players and more, symphonies of ninety minutes, harmony stretched to the edge of tonality. mahler wants the symphony to contain the world; strauss can make muted, flutter-tongued brass bleat like a flock of sheep; rachmaninoff builds melodies from chant and bells; sibelius goes the other way, toward compression and silence. progressive tonality orchestral song tone poem enharmonic reinterpretation added sixth pedal point heterophony

title: The French Line
sub: 1870–1937 · Colour, clarity and the escape from Wagner
k: the french line 1870–1937 · colour, clarity and the escape from wagner chords heard as colour, scales drawn from chant, from java and from the whole-tone collection; orchestration as a precise art of timbre. faure refines, debussy dissolves, satie subtracts, and ravel engineers. planing whole-tone collection anhemitonic pentatonic scale modal harmony melodie arabesque orchestral transcription

title: Modernism
sub: 1908–1945 · Breaking the key, the beat and the frame
k: modernism 1908–1945 · breaking the key, the beat and the frame in 1908 schoenberg writes music without a tonal centre; in 1913 stravinsky’s rite of spring makes rhythm the main event. then come twelve-tone rows, folk music recorded on wax cylinders by bartok, neoclassicism, and composers like prokofiev and shostakovich writing under the eye of the state. atonality twelve-note row sprechstimme polyrhythm additive metre neoclassicism polymodality ostinato

title: After 1945
sub: 1945–present · Total control, chance, texture, pulse — and then everything at once
k: after 1945 1945–present · total control, chance, texture, pulse — and then everything at once after the war: serialism extended to every parameter, then ligeti’s clouds of sound, feldman’s long quiet, reich’s pulse and phase, part’s bells, and the spectral music of saariaho, built from the physics of a single tone. many styles, many workshops. integral serialism indeterminacy musique concrete micropolyphony phase shifting spectralism tintinnabuli extended technique

title: A Dance to the Music of Time
k: a dance to the music of time nicolas poussin · c. 1634–36 the baroque shared context father time plays a lyre while four figures dance in a ring. poussin made the picture in rome for giulio rospigliosi, the future pope clement ix, who also wrote opera librettos. the connection to baroque music is both institutional and technical: an educated patron receives an allegory whose cyclical movement is made legible by measured gestures. the wallace collection record gives its date and provenance.

title: A Song for St Cecilia’s Day — opening
k: a song for st cecilia’s day — opening john dryden · 1687 the baroque documented use these lines turn the ordering of the elements into a musical act. handel set the poem in his ode for st cecilia’s day, hwv 76, in 1739; later stanzas summon particular instruments and the passions attributed to them. the public-domain text supplies a direct example of musical rhetoric.

title: An Experiment on a Bird in the Air Pump
k: an experiment on a bird in the air pump joseph wright of derby · 1768 classical editorial comparison a scientific demonstration becomes a scene of differentiated attention: the children fear for the bird, one spectator watches the mechanism, and others turn inward or towards one another. the comparison with a mozart ensemble concerns the organisation of simultaneous responses. both give several viewpoints a shared frame. the national gallery identifies the bird as a cockatoo and describes the experiment’s place in public scientific demonstration.

title: An die Freude — first stanza
k: an die freude — first stanza friedrich schiller · 1785; revised c. 1803 classical documented use schiller’s revised stanza, with spelling modernised, replaces the first version’s explicit pairing of beggars and princes with “all people”. beethoven set selections from the revised poem in the ninth symphony, adding his own introductory appeal, “o freunde, nicht diese tone!” the finale tests fraternity through changes of musical company: bass soloist, quartet, chorus and orchestra. the historical versions record the poem’s revisions.

title: The Abbey in the Oakwood
k: the abbey in the oakwood caspar david friedrich · 1809–10 romanticism editorial comparison the funeral procession occupies only a narrow strip beneath the ruined gothic window and leafless oaks. architecture survives as a fragment, while the implied ceremony gives the small figures a temporal direction. the pairing concerns the same romantic interest in ruins, memory and the incomplete that informs the song cycle and character piece. the museum’s friedrich project documents the painting and its pendant, monk by the sea.

title: Erlkönig — opening stanzas
k: erlkonig — opening stanzas johann wolfgang von goethe · 1782 romanticism documented use schubert’s 1815 setting, d 328, distributes the speakers by register and harmonic character while the piano’s repeated triplets maintain the ride. the father explains away what the child sees; the accompaniment refuses to relax when he does so. the final interruption of the running texture makes the narrator’s report physically different from everything preceding it. goethe’s original is a ballad.

title: The Scream
k: the scream edvard munch · 1893 fin de siecle editorial comparison the rigid diagonal of the walkway meets curves that pass through sky, water and the central figure. munch makes an experience alter the organisation of the visible scene. the comparison with late-romantic music concerns that transfer between individual perception and an enlarged surrounding field: an orchestral texture can change the apparent meaning of a simple melodic figure. this is the national museum’s 1893 version.

title: The midnight song from Also sprach Zarathustra
sub: Friedrich Nietzsche · 1884; repeated in Part IV, 1885
k: the midnight song from also sprach zarathustra friedrich nietzsche · 1884; repeated in part iv, 1885 fin de siecle documented use mahler sets this text for alto in the fourth movement of the third symphony; strauss responds to the larger book in also sprach zarathustra. the words first appear at the end of “das andere tanzlied” in part iii. the intervening numbered strokes of midnight are omitted here. nietzsche’s opposition between grief, delight and recurrence gives the musical return a philosophical subject.

title: Bathers at Asnières
k: bathers at asnieres georges seurat · 1884, retouched c. 1887 the french line editorial comparison seurat built his colour from separate touches meant to combine in the viewer’s eye, following the colour theory of chevreul and ogden rood; when he reworked this canvas around 1887 he added small dots of complementary colour to the boy’s hat and the water. the affinity with debussy and ravel lies in their orchestral colour: they repeatedly set pure colours side by side — a flute’s low register beside muted horns, a harp harmonic on a string chord — so that the blend happens in the ear.

title: Art poétique — first and fourth stanzas
sub: Paul Verlaine · written 1874; published in Jadis et naguère, 1884
k: art poetique — first and fourth stanzas paul verlaine · written 1874; published in jadis et naguere, 1884 the french line editorial comparison a manifesto in nine-syllable lines — l’impair, the odd count verlaine recommends, which cannot divide into the symmetrical halves of the classical alexandrine. the musical analogue is the french line’s distrust of four-square phrasing and emphatic arrival. verlaine was the poet these composers set most: faure’s la bonne chanson and cinq melodies “de venise”, debussy’s ariettes oubliees and two sets of fetes galantes.

title: Fate of the Animals
k: fate of the animals franz marc · 1913 modernism shared context intersecting diagonals break the forest and animals into recognisable planes that disrupt ordinary depth. marc belonged to the blue rider circle whose publications also included schoenberg’s work. the painting predates the first world war. its present surface includes paul klee’s 1919 restoration of damage sustained in a 1917 fire, documented by the kunstmuseum basel.

title: Zone — opening
k: zone — opening guillaume apollinaire · 1913, in alcools modernism editorial comparison the opening gives a steel tower the role of a shepherdess and brings bridges, antiquity and motorcars into successive lines without punctuation. that assembly of incompatible registers offers a concrete literary counterpart to musical collage and abrupt changes of block. the 1913 collection places “zone” first, making its argument with the past the reader’s point of entry.

title: Broadway Boogie Woogie
k: broadway boogie woogie piet mondrian · 1942–43 after 1945 editorial comparison the grid provides a stable division while short coloured units interrupt its continuity, making the eye compare repetition and displacement. its musical title refers to boogie-woogie, which mondrian encountered in new york after arriving in 1940. the moma record documents that setting. postwar process music addresses a related technical problem: keeping the underlying unit recognisable while its combinations change. the link to reich is a comparison of technique, with no documented influence.

title: Walden — from “Sounds”
k: walden — from “sounds” henry david thoreau · 1854 after 1945 editorial comparison the passage makes unallocated time a positive condition. cage drew on thoreau’s journal to construct empty words in 1973–74, progressively removing linguistic units until letters and sounds became the material. this passage from walden offers an earlier statement of a related attention. see digital thoreau’s text and the john cage trust account.

title: Les Plaisirs du bal
k: les plaisirs du bal jean-antoine watteau · c. 1715–17 francois couperin shared context a dancer performs before a seated company while musicians occupy the architectural setting. the painting dates from the years of couperin’s first two harpsichord books, whose dances and social portraits similarly depend on a small audience’s knowledge of gesture and deportment. the link is their shared parisian culture. watch the difference between the central dance and the spectators’ individual poses; listen for the comparable distinction between a piece’s dance pattern and its local ornaments.

title: Pèlerinage à l’île de Cythère
k: pelerinage a l’ile de cythere jean-antoine watteau · 1717 francois couperin shared context watteau submitted this painting to the academie royale in 1717; its lovers and theatrical landscape helped establish the category fete galante. couperin’s second harpsichord book appeared in the same year. both works belong to a culture in which pastoral costume and gestures of courtship could be presented as art for private spectators. no documented programme connects this painting with les barricades mysterieuses. thomas ades documented use this is a direct source for l’embarquement, the fifth movement of arcadiana. watteau’s couples occupy the island associated with venus while the ship and attendant cupids make departure part of the image. ades places the movement among the quartet’s aquatic scenes; its high string writing and changing figuration also glance towards debussy’s l’isle joyeuse. the reference concerns an idyll already in the act of disappearing.

title: Bacino di San Marco, Venice
k: bacino di san marco, venice canaletto · 1738 antonio vivaldi shared context the basin and its boats place venice’s ceremonial buildings within a working system of transport and trade. canaletto painted such views for an international market that included travellers who also heard the city’s institutional concerts. the pieta stood on the waterfront east of the piazza san marco. this is vivaldi’s urban and commercial setting; the building now called the pieta’s church was erected after his death.

title: La Primavera
sub: Anonymous; sometimes attributed to Vivaldi · Published with Op. 8, 1725
k: la primavera anonymous; sometimes attributed to vivaldi · published with op. 8, 1725 antonio vivaldi documented use the sonnet’s first eight lines belong to the opening allegro, the next three to the largo, and the final three to the pastoral dance. in the original publication, lettered references connect these events to the parts. the poem documents the programme. the philharmonie de paris’s account of spring follows these correspondences.

title: Title page of Nouveau système de musique théorique
sub: Jean-Philippe Rameau; printed by Jean-Baptiste-Christophe Ballard · 1726
k: title page of nouveau systeme de musique theorique jean-philippe rameau; printed by jean-baptiste-christophe ballard · 1726 jean-philippe rameau shared context the 1726 nouveau systeme followed the traite de l’harmonie of 1722. the title promises principles for accompaniment and composition, linking speculative explanation to the daily tasks of a working musician. rameau continued revising his theoretical account. the library of congress copy preserves the page reproduced here.

title: Phèdre — Act I, scene 3
k: phedre — act i, scene 3 jean racine · 1677 jean-philippe rameau documented use pellegrin’s hippolyte et aricie draws on racine’s tragedy; these lines belong to the play alone. racine makes phedre recount desire through failures of bodily control; the opera redistributes the story among recitative, supernatural scenes, dances and a surviving pair of lovers. pellegrin discusses his debt and his alterations in the 1733 libretto’s preface.

title: Johann Sebastian Bach
k: johann sebastian bach elias gottlob haussmann · 1746 johann sebastian bach shared context the paper in bach’s hand is the canon triplex a 6 voci, bwv 1076: three written lines generate six sounding parts by canonic imitation. the portrait displays his compositional craft. bach joined lorenz christoph mizler’s corresponding society of the musical sciences in 1747; the canon also belongs to the learned exchange associated with that society. haussmann painted a second version in 1748, now held by the bach-archiv.

title: St Thomas’s Church and School, Leipzig
k: st thomas’s church and school, leipzig johann gottfried krugner · 1723 johann sebastian bach shared context the view places church and school side by side: bach’s principal musical workplace and the institution that housed and trained his singers. his family lived in the thomasschule. the arrangement matters to the cantatas: the same establishment supplied education, accommodation, rehearsal and the labour of preparing music for the city’s churches. the engraving dates from the year of his arrival in leipzig.

title: Aus tiefer Not schrei ich zu dir — first stanza
k: aus tiefer not schrei ich zu dir — first stanza martin luther · 1524 johann sebastian bach documented use luther’s paraphrase of psalm 130 supplies the chorale of cantata bwv 38 and two organ settings in clavier-ubung iii. in bwv 686 bach writes six parts, including two for the pedals: the hymn is embedded in a texture whose sustained notes and imitative preparation recall older vocal polyphony. the german text is given in modernised spelling; the published hymn predates bach by two centuries.

title: Wachet auf, ruft uns die Stimme — opening lines
k: wachet auf, ruft uns die stimme — opening lines philipp nicolai · 1599 johann sebastian bach documented use nicolai published words and melody in 1599. bach’s bwv 140, first performed in 1731, uses all three stanzas of the hymn, with new poetry between them developing the bridal imagery. in the opening chorus the sopranos carry nicolai’s melody in long notes above active lower voices; in the fourth movement the tenors sing the second stanza against an independent string melody. the hymn refers to the parable of the wise and foolish virgins in matthew 25.

title: Captain Thomas Coram
k: captain thomas coram william hogarth · 1740 george frideric handel shared context coram founded the foundling hospital in 1739. hogarth donated this portrait and encouraged other artists to support the institution, helping make it a public destination for painting. handel’s benefit performances added music to the same philanthropic project. his 1749 benefit introduced the foundling hospital anthem; messiah followed there in 1750. the foundling museum’s collection preserves the material connection.

title: Westminster Bridge, with the Lord Mayor’s Procession on the Thames
k: westminster bridge, with the lord mayor’s procession on the thames canaletto · 1747 george frideric handel shared context the procession displays the river as a route for public ceremony, with decorated barges, spectators and the city’s new bridge. painted thirty years after the documented water music excursion, it shows the continuing civic practice that makes a floating royal concert intelligible: the thames could function as an auditorium as well as a commercial waterway.

title: Alexander’s Feast — closing stanza
k: alexander’s feast — closing stanza john dryden · 1697 george frideric handel documented use timotheus has used music to manipulate alexander’s emotions; saint cecilia’s sacred music supplies the final comparison. handel set dryden’s ode in 1736, with adaptations by newburgh hamilton. the closing antithesis becomes a choral judgement after an evening in which musical affects have been demonstrated one by one. the 1697 text supplies the work’s literary source.

title: Bárbara de Braganza as Princess of Asturias
k: barbara de braganza as princess of asturias jean ranc · c. 1729 domenico scarlatti shared context maria barbara’s marriage carried scarlatti’s employment from portugal to spain. the portrait presents her dynastic position, while the sonatas record a different part of her education: the keyboard skills cultivated through a long association with her teacher. her ownership of instruments and manuscript music directly links the sitter to the repertory.

title: Portrait group: The singer Farinelli and friends
k: portrait group: the singer farinelli and friends jacopo amigoni · c. 1750–52 domenico scarlatti shared context farinelli appears with the singer teresa castellini, the poet metastasio and amigoni himself. the group is a constructed image of friendship; a joint sitting in madrid remains undocumented. farinelli and scarlatti served the same spanish royal household, and farinelli’s later collection is part of the history of the sonata manuscripts. the ngv’s painting makes the court’s connections among singing, poetry, collecting and painting visible.

title: To the reader of the Essercizi — opening sentence
k: to the reader of the essercizi — opening sentence domenico scarlatti · 1738–39 domenico scarlatti documented use the preface addresses both kinds of player and names a practical purpose: freedom and assurance at the instrument. the phrase belongs to scarlatti’s own publication; the cat story attached to k. 30 came later. the text is quoted in the treccani account; spelling and capitalisation are normalised here.

title: Flute Concert of Frederick the Great at Sanssouci
k: flute concert of frederick the great at sanssouci adolph menzel · 1850–52 carl philipp emanuel bach shared context menzel reconstructs the court where bach earned his salary: frederick plays the flute, and bach is seated at the keyboard. painted a century after the events, this is historical theatre. its arrangement makes the employment relationship visible. in the picture, the accompanist watches the royal soloist, while the listeners occupy the room around them.

title: Die Ehre Gottes aus der Natur — first stanza
k: die ehre gottes aus der natur — first stanza christian furchtegott gellert · 1757 carl philipp emanuel bach documented use bach set gellert’s geistliche oden und lieder in 1758; beethoven returned to six of the same poet’s religious texts in op. 48. gellert’s short clauses and scriptural imagery offer a different task from operatic recitative: clear delivery for a domestic singer without making the accompaniment inert. text: the 1757 collection.

title: Versuch — the performer’s feeling
sub: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach · 1753, Part I, chapter 3, §13
k: versuch — the performer’s feeling carl philipp emanuel bach · 1753, part i, chapter 3, §13 carl philipp emanuel bach shared context the prose belongs to the eighteenth-century discussion of acting and sensibility as much as to keyboard instruction. bach’s next sentences distinguish languid or sorrowful passages from forceful or cheerful ones: the performer’s expression must change with them. the digital versuch supplies the passage in its original context.

title: Eszterháza Palace, Fertőd
k: eszterhaza palace, fertod unidentified photographer · 1920 joseph haydn shared context a later photograph of the palace complex where haydn composed, rehearsed and directed opera for prince nikolaus. the image records the scale of the establishment. court musicians worked within a household that also maintained servants, gardens, theatres and ceremonial rooms; haydn’s symphonies and baryton trios were part of that system of daily expenditure.

title: The Ancient of Days, frontispiece to Europe a Prophecy
k: the ancient of days, frontispiece to europe a prophecy william blake · 1794 joseph haydn shared context blake’s figure measures the world with compasses while haydn’s oratorio makes an ordered world emerge through harmony. contact is undocumented. blake’s urizen can represent restrictive rational law, whereas haydn’s chorus celebrates creation. the print was made during haydn’s second london visit, placing these opposed accounts of cosmic order in the same decade and city.

title: Paradise Lost, Book VII — before the creation of humanity
k: paradise lost, book vii — before the creation of humanity john milton · 1667; revised edition 1674 joseph haydn documented use milton, genesis and the psalms supplied the english source libretto that van swieten adapted for the creation. the passage moves from populated earth to the upright human figure, the same transition heard before haydn’s tenor aria mit wurd’ und hoheit angetan. text: book vii.

title: The Mozart Family in Paris
k: the mozart family in paris louis carrogis carmontelle · 1763 wolfgang amadeus mozart shared context leopold plays the violin beside wolfgang at the keyboard while maria anna stands with music. the drawing records the family’s paris visit during the long tour of 1763–66. the child composer appears within a working ensemble managed by his father. nannerl’s place in the group also restores the sibling partnership often removed from accounts of the tour.

title: The Hall of Stars in the Palace of the Queen of the Night
sub: Karl Friedrich Thiele, after Karl Friedrich Schinkel · 1847–49, after the 1816 stage design
k: the hall of stars in the palace of the queen of the night karl friedrich thiele, after karl friedrich schinkel · 1847–49, after the 1816 stage design wolfgang amadeus mozart documented use schinkel designed the setting for the berlin magic flute of 1816; this print belongs to a later publication of his designs. the queen occupies a celestial architecture that gives visual form to the separation already audible between her high coloratura and the lower voices of the other characters. it documents the opera’s nineteenth-century staging history, after the 1791 premiere. museum catalogue.

title: Das Veilchen — opening
k: das veilchen — opening johann wolfgang von goethe · 1774; published 1775 wolfgang amadeus mozart documented use mozart set the poem as k. 476 on 8 june 1785. the violet’s imagined speech and the girl’s unknowing destruction of it turn the song into a small dramatic scene; mozart adds the final exclamation das arme veilchen! the excerpt gives goethe’s opening with modernised spelling. kochel catalogue record.

title: Le nozze di Figaro — forgiveness in the final scene
k: le nozze di figaro — forgiveness in the final scene lorenzo da ponte · 1786 wolfgang amadeus mozart documented use the count has just refused the forgiveness that he now needs himself. mozart slows the action for the countess’s answer and then allows the ensemble to take up its harmony. the words establish the reversal of power; the sustained musical response gives it a duration beyond ordinary dialogue. text: the 1786 vienna libretto.

title: Bonaparte Crossing the Great St Bernard Pass
k: bonaparte crossing the great st bernard pass jacques-louis david · 1800–01 ludwig van beethoven shared context david turns the crossing into a public image of command: bonaparte points forward while the names of earlier conquerors appear on the rock. beethoven’s changing relation to bonaparte during the making of the eroica belongs to the same period of heroic image-making. the link is the political icon whose name could be written into, and then removed from, a title page; there is no evidence that the painting supplied the symphony’s programme.

title: Title page of the Eroica score, with Bonaparte’s name erased
sub: Copyist, with alterations by Ludwig van Beethoven · 1804
k: title page of the eroica score, with bonaparte’s name erased copyist, with alterations by ludwig van beethoven · 1804 ludwig van beethoven documented use this is the surviving copyist’s score with beethoven’s corrections; the autograph score is lost. the erasure damages the paper where the title referred to bonaparte. ferdinand ries’s later account supplies the scene of beethoven’s anger; the manuscript supplies independent physical evidence of the changed wording. later annotations record further changes to the leaf. archive account.

title: Heiligenstadt Testament — art and survival
sub: Ludwig van Beethoven · 6 October 1802; postscript 10 October
k: heiligenstadt testament — art and survival ludwig van beethoven · 6 october 1802; postscript 10 october ludwig van beethoven shared context the unsent document addresses beethoven’s brothers and explains conduct that others had interpreted as hostility. this excerpt concerns his decision to continue living and working. the original is held by the staats- und universitatsbibliothek hamburg. spelling and punctuation are lightly regularised here. german text.

title: An die Freude — opening stanza
k: an die freude — opening stanza friedrich schiller · 1785; revised 1803 ludwig van beethoven documented use beethoven selected and reordered parts of schiller’s poem for the ninth. ‘all human beings become brothers’ belongs to the revised wording; the earlier version spoke of beggars becoming brothers of princes. beethoven supplied the bass soloist’s introductory o freunde, nicht diese tone!. textual versions.

title: Ein Schubert-Abend bei Josef von Spaun (A Schubert Evening at Josef von Spaun’s)
k: ein schubert-abend bei josef von spaun (a schubert evening at josef von spaun’s) moritz von schwind · 1868 franz schubert shared context schwind places schubert at the piano with vogl beside him and the circle of friends arranged as listeners. the drawing was made forty years after the composer’s death; its crowded room commemorates that circle. it identifies the social machinery behind the songs: a pianist-composer, an experienced singer and friends who supplied poems, rooms, introductions and subscriptions. the museum catalogue records the mixed drawing technique.

title: Winter Landscape
k: winter landscape caspar david friedrich · probably 1811 franz schubert editorial comparison a man has put aside his crutches beside a boulder and prays before a crucifix; beyond the fir trees, a gothic church emerges through mist. the link with winterreise is shared subject matter. friedrich gives his solitary traveller a religious object towards which to turn. muller’s walker in das wirtshaus approaches a cemetery as an inn, finds no room there and must continue. the national gallery’s account identifies the painting’s christian signs of renewal: a different outcome from the song cycle’s unanswered final question.

title: Der Leiermann — first and last stanzas
sub: Wilhelm Müller · Published 1823; collected 1824; set by Schubert 1827
k: der leiermann — first and last stanzas wilhelm muller · published 1823; collected 1824; set by schubert 1827 franz schubert documented use the three middle stanzas are omitted. the leier here is a hurdy-gurdy, a string instrument sounded by a hand-turned wheel. its drone allows the musical act to persist without a change of harmony. muller ends with two questions, which remain unanswered in schubert’s setting. the 1824 text and publication history distinguish muller’s wording from small changes in the song.

title: Marguerite with the Spinning Wheel, from the Faust illustrations
k: marguerite with the spinning wheel, from the faust illustrations eugene delacroix · 1828 hector berlioz shared context delacroix’s seventeen faust lithographs accompanied albert stapfer’s french translation in 1828. berlioz read gerard de nerval’s translation that year and composed his huit scenes de faust in 1828–29. the two artists approached goethe independently: marguerite’s enclosed room and repetitive labour oppose faust’s restless movement. in la damnation, her solitary songs similarly arrest the succession of public scenes.

title: Romeo and Juliet · Act III, scene 5
k: romeo and juliet · act iii, scene 5 william shakespeare · first published 1597 hector berlioz documented use juliet tries to misidentify the sound that requires romeo to leave. berlioz saw harriet smithson as juliet in 1827. his 1839 dramatic symphony transfers the lovers’ dialogue to the orchestra, asking instruments to distinguish appeal, interruption and consent without words. the play’s dependence on heard signals makes that transfer unusually exact.

title: Aeneid · IV, 651–654
k: aeneid · iv, 651–654 virgil · first century bce hector berlioz documented use dido addresses the objects aeneas has left behind. berlioz read this scene as a child and made her farewell the centre of the final act of les troyens. in his own french adaptation, private leave-taking expands into the carthaginians’ curse and a vision of rome.

title: Fanny Mendelssohn
k: fanny mendelssohn wilhelm hensel · 1829 fanny hensel documented encounter wilhelm drew fanny in the year they married, with a floral wreath and carefully articulated dress. his drawings later shared the pages of the illustrated manuscript of das jahr. their collaboration belongs to the material history of the music.

title: Nachts · set as Nachtwanderer
sub: Joseph von Eichendorff · Published 1826; Hensel’s setting published 1847
k: nachts · set as nachtwanderer joseph von eichendorff · published 1826; hensel’s setting published 1847 fanny hensel documented use hensel’s op. 7 no. 1 gives the poem a piano part whose continuing motion complicates the repeated claims of stillness. the final ‘rufen’ is a call from dreams. the sung german text supplies a precise point of comparison with robert schumann’s different eichendorff settings.

title: Staffa, Fingal’s Cave
k: staffa, fingal’s cave j. m. w. turner · 1831–32; exhibited 1832 felix mendelssohn shared context turner visited staffa in 1831, two years after mendelssohn. his painting includes a steamship: romantic access to the apparently remote landscape depended on modern transport. the overture and painting are independent responses to the same hebridean destination. turner blurs sea, smoke and atmosphere; mendelssohn keeps a precisely articulated motif audible while its orchestral surroundings change. collection record.

title: A Midsummer Night’s Dream · Act V, scene 1
k: a midsummer night’s dream · act v, scene 1 william shakespeare · first published 1600 felix mendelssohn documented use puck’s epilogue supplies a theatrical exit from confusion. mendelssohn’s 1842 incidental score returns to the 1826 overture’s wind chords at the end, making musical recollection serve a comparable closing function. the quick string writing belongs to a play that repeatedly changes the status of what its characters think they have seen.

title: Study for the Double Portrait of Chopin and George Sand
k: study for the double portrait of chopin and george sand eugene delacroix · c. 1838 frederic chopin documented encounter the drawing preserves the shared composition lost when the unfinished oil painting was cut apart. chopin plays; sand occupies the same space as a listener and working companion. delacroix knew both and later visited nohant. the study records their artistic circle at first hand. louvre catalogue.

title: George Sand
k: george sand eugene delacroix · 1838 frederic chopin shared context the other surviving fragment of the portrait shown above the biography. separating the canvases turned a scene of music-making into two independent images of famous people. sand’s nohant household supplied working conditions for the mature sonatas, barcarolle and polonaise-fantaisie; her accounts of chopin’s revisions are valuable evidence, though they are written by a novelist involved in the events.

title: Wiosna · opening three stanzas
sub: Stefan Witwicki · Set by Chopin in 1838
k: wiosna · opening three stanzas stefan witwicki · set by chopin in 1838 frederic chopin documented use chopin set this poem as wiosna, later published as op. 74 no. 2. these are the first three stanzas; the poem subsequently turns towards an unexplained sorrow and a lark’s ascending song. his small body of polish songs connects his music directly to emigre poetry. polish sung text.

title: Man and Woman Contemplating the Moon
k: man and woman contemplating the moon caspar david friedrich · c. 1824 robert schumann editorial comparison the two figures share a landscape whose nocturnal world invites comparison with eichendorff’s poems, especially mondnacht, which schumann set in op. 39. the exposed tree roots and interrupted path give the view a physical resistance; in the song, the piano’s continuous movement and the voice’s slower phrases similarly occupy different measures of time.

title: Im wunderschönen Monat Mai
sub: Heinrich Heine · 1822–23; collected in Buch der Lieder, 1827
k: im wunderschonen monat mai heinrich heine · 1822–23; collected in buch der lieder, 1827 robert schumann documented use schumann opens dichterliebe with this poem in 1840. heine reports the confession but gives no answer from the beloved; schumann makes the absence audible by withholding a final tonic resolution. the simple equation of spring and love is therefore unstable before the cycle has reached its explicit disappointments. 1827 text and scan.

title: Beethovens Instrumentalmusik · from Kreisleriana
sub: E. T. A. Hoffmann · Collected in 1814
k: beethovens instrumentalmusik · from kreisleriana e. t. a. hoffmann · collected in 1814 robert schumann shared context hoffmann’s essays and fictions give the musician johannes kreisler a voice at once analytical and unstable. schumann borrowed the name for op. 16. the rapid alternation of agitation and inward reflection has a literary counterpart in hoffmann’s changes of speaker and frame. this passage is quoted from the beethoven essay.

title: The Marriage of the Virgin (Lo Sposalizio)
k: the marriage of the virgin (lo sposalizio) raphael · 1504 franz liszt documented use the direct source for sposalizio, the first piece of the italian annees. raphael’s central temple and radiating pavement give the crowded ceremony a strict perspective. liszt’s small opening idea expands through repetition and harmonic enlargement until it can sustain a ceremonial climax. the connection is named in the score.

title: Lorenzo de’ Medici, called Il Pensieroso
sub: Michelangelo; photograph by an unidentified photographer · Sculpture, c. 1526–34; photograph, c. 1875–1900
k: lorenzo de’ medici, called il pensieroso michelangelo; photograph by an unidentified photographer · sculpture, c. 1526–34; photograph, c. 1875–1900 franz liszt documented use the helmeted, seated figure from the tomb of lorenzo, duke of urbino, supplied the title of liszt’s il penseroso. its low register, dotted tread and chromatic harmonies make a deliberate contrast with the preceding sposalizio. liszt also printed michelangelo’s four-line answer to a poem about the adjacent figure of night: he connected the chapel’s sculpture with sleep, stone and the wish not to be awakened.

title: Pace non trovo — opening quatrain
sub: Francesco Petrarca · Fourteenth century; Liszt’s Sonetto 104
k: pace non trovo — opening quatrain francesco petrarca · fourteenth century; liszt’s sonetto 104 franz liszt documented use the opening of sonnet 134 in the modern numbering, called 104 in liszt’s edition. the contradictory verbs give a reason for the music’s changes between declamation, sustained song and sudden agitation. liszt’s piano setting is descended from his vocal one: the decorated right-hand line becomes an instrumental singer.

title: Portrait of Alessandro Manzoni
k: portrait of alessandro manzoni francesco hayez · 1841 giuseppe verdi shared context the writer whose death prompted verdi’s requiem. hayez portrays the author of i promessi sposi through the sitter’s hands and direct bearing. verdi admired manzoni’s literary and moral standing and conducted the memorial work on the first anniversary of his death. the connection is a named dedication and public act of remembrance. brera collection record.

title: Othello and Desdemona in Venice
k: othello and desdemona in venice theodore chasseriau · 1850 giuseppe verdi shared context chasseriau depicts othello telling desdemona his life, a subject drawn from shakespeare’s first act. boito removed that venetian act when adapting otello, but its account of their courtship returns in the love duet at the end of verdi’s act i. the lovers remember that she loved him for his suffering and he loved her for her pity. the painting supplies a visible setting for a past that the opera reconstructs through sung recollection. louvre collection record.

title: Macbeth, Act V, scene 5 — “Tomorrow”
k: macbeth, act v, scene 5 — “tomorrow” william shakespeare · c. 1606; first published 1623 giuseppe verdi documented use macbeth speaks after learning of his wife’s death. verdi and piave compress the response into brief declamation; macbeth’s principal late aria, “pieta, rispetto, amore”, has already occurred. the comparison shows adaptation as a change of dramatic timing. shakespeare suspends the battle for an argument about time, while the opera must decide how much musical duration that suspension can bear.

title: The Frolic of the Rhine-Maidens
k: the frolic of the rhine-maidens arthur rackham · 1910 richard wagner shared context rackham’s illustration belongs to an edition of wagner’s own dramas. the swimming figures and curling water answer the beginning of rheingold, where the stage is submerged and the orchestra is still emerging from its sustained e♭. the book makes visible the physical setting from which the gold is stolen; wagner’s later motifs keep recalling that loss after the scene has changed.

title: Tristram and Isolde
k: tristram and isolde edmund blair leighton · exhibited 1907 richard wagner editorial comparison leighton exhibited this parallel treatment of the medieval legend at the royal academy in 1907, decades after the opera. its historical costume fixes the lovers in a visible medieval setting; wagner’s second act strips much of that social world away through darkness and the lovers’ argument against “day”. the image’s legible bodies contrast with the music’s unsettled harmony.

title: Im Treibhaus — opening stanzas
k: im treibhaus — opening stanzas mathilde wesendonck · 1858 richard wagner documented use wagner labelled this song a study for tristan und isolde; its material is connected with the desolate prelude to act iii. the greenhouse gives the poem a precise condition: living things have been transported from their native climate and cannot return. the first two of six stanzas are quoted here; the complete german text carries the comparison into human exile.

title: Hans Sachs’s Wahn monologue — opening
sub: Richard Wagner · Libretto completed 1862; opera completed 1867
k: hans sachs’s wahn monologue — opening richard wagner · libretto completed 1862; opera completed 1867 richard wagner documented use in act iii of die meistersinger, the cobbler-poet reads the previous night’s street fight as an instance of recurrent human delusion. the orchestral recollections make his monologue an interpretation of music the audience has already heard. his decision to redirect this irrational energy into the song contest links the work’s comic action to its argument about making art.

title: Robert and Clara Schumann
sub: After Ernst Rietschel; reproductive artist unidentified · Reproduced in 1918
k: robert and clara schumann after ernst rietschel; reproductive artist unidentified · reproduced in 1918 clara schumann shared context rietschel belonged to the schumanns’ dresden circle. the double profile gives their marriage a single commemorative object; clara’s separate performance history extends for forty years beyond robert’s death. read the paired image alongside the joint ruckert publication, where individually authored songs share a title page. the reproduction’s source is documented; its reproductive artist remains unidentified.

title: Liebst du um Schönheit
sub: Friedrich Rückert · From Liebesfrühling; Clara’s setting 1841
k: liebst du um schonheit friedrich ruckert · from liebesfruhling; clara’s setting 1841 clara schumann documented use clara’s op. 12 no. 2 belongs to the 1841 collection she published with robert. three stanzas reject an external reason for love; the fourth changes ‘nicht’ to ‘ja’. that verbal alteration makes a small musical change carry a large formal consequence. mahler set the same poem much later, in 1902: the shared text invites comparison of the two settings. german text and work identification.

title: St Florian Abbey
sub: Georg Matthäus Vischer · 1677 edition; first published 1674
k: st florian abbey georg matthaus vischer · 1677 edition; first published 1674 anton bruckner shared context the abbey where bruckner became a choirboy in 1837, later worked as teacher and organist, and was buried in 1896. vischer’s engraving records the institution and its setting before the baroque rebuilding. behind the familiar “cathedral in sound” metaphor stand the actual buildings and daily musical work that formed him.

title: Anton Bruckner and Richard Wagner
k: anton bruckner and richard wagner otto bohler · c. 1885 anton bruckner shared context bohler shows bruckner accepting snuff from wagner. the caricature records the public image of the deferential admirer, an image encouraged by the third symphony’s dedication. bruckner’s contrapuntal finales and three-group sonata expositions belong to his independent symphonic practice; the print documents his reception.

title: Locus iste
sub: Roman Catholic liturgy · Traditional Latin gradual; Bruckner’s setting, 1869
k: locus iste roman catholic liturgy · traditional latin gradual; bruckner’s setting, 1869 anton bruckner documented use the text belongs to the dedication of a church. bruckner composed his four-part unaccompanied setting, wab 23, in connection with the dedication celebrations for the votive chapel of linz’s new cathedral in 1869. its c major opening is predominantly chordal; the middle phrase introduces chromatic movement before the opening returns. a few minutes of vocal writing expose the same management of stability, departure and return that the symphonies enlarge.

title: On the Seashore (Modern Iphigenia)
k: on the seashore (modern iphigenia) anselm feuerbach · 1875 johannes brahms shared context brahms composed nanie, op. 82, after the death of his friend feuerbach in 1880 and dedicated it to the painter’s stepmother, henriette. its schiller text invokes greek myth and the death of beauty, a subject appropriate to feuerbach’s repeated engagement with classical figures. the isolated iphigenia provides a visual counterpart to that classicising language.

title: Ritter Tod, from Brahmsphantasie
k: ritter tod, from brahmsphantasie max klinger · 1894 johannes brahms documented encounter klinger’s brahmsphantasie places prints alongside brahms’s songs and the schicksalslied, treating music and image as interacting parts of a book. brahms received the completed work in 1894. this is a contemporary artist’s direct response to his music. the met’s impression preserves the varied print techniques through which klinger distinguishes line, darkness and atmospheric depth.

title: Nänie
sub: Friedrich Schiller · 1800; set by Brahms in 1880–81
k: nanie friedrich schiller · 1800; set by brahms in 1880–81 johannes brahms documented use schiller’s elegiac couplets allude to eurydice’s loss, adonis’s wound and achilles’s death. brahms’s d major setting answers the opening declaration with flowing oboe writing and imitative choral entries. near the end he returns to the penultimate line about survival in a lament: the music itself enacts that restricted form of remembrance. german text.

title: Hyperions Schicksalslied — first stanza
sub: Friedrich Hölderlin · 1799; set by Brahms in 1868–71
k: hyperions schicksalslied — first stanza friedrich holderlin · 1799; set by brahms in 1868–71 johannes brahms documented use the opening stanza describes beings exempt from human suffering; the poem later drops into the blind, repeated falling of mortal lives. brahms’s schicksalslied, op. 54, opposes a slow e♭ major opening to an agitated c minor section. its wordless c major postlude returns to the opening music after the poem has ended, offering an instrumental response that holderlin’s final words do not supply.

title: Portrait of Modest Mussorgsky
k: portrait of modest mussorgsky ilya repin · 1881 modest mussorgsky documented encounter repin painted the composer in the nikolaevsky military hospital shortly before his death. the open hospital gown, uncombed hair and direct gaze exclude the conventions of the official composer portrait. repin and mussorgsky belonged to overlapping artistic circles around stasov; the painting records their encounter.

title: Project for a City Gate in Kyiv
k: project for a city gate in kyiv viktor hartmann · 1869 modest mussorgsky documented use hartmann’s unbuilt gate, with its helmet-shaped tower, bell chamber and large central arch, supplied mussorgsky with a proposal for public architecture. the final picture combines a broad e♭ major theme, a quieter chant-like passage and bell textures; the promenade’s returning material places the observer inside that imagined ceremony.

title: Canary-chick costumes for Trilby
k: canary-chick costumes for trilby viktor hartmann · 1871 modest mussorgsky documented use hartmann designed eggshell costumes for children in julius gerber’s ballet trilby, choreographed by marius petipa. mussorgsky’s ballet of the unhatched chicks translates a theatrical contrivance into high-register staccato figures, grace notes and trills. the shell is part of a dancer’s costume: the source is already an artifice before music transforms it.

title: Tatyana’s letter, from Eugene Onegin
k: tatyana’s letter, from eugene onegin alexander pushkin · chapter iii, published 1827 pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky documented use tchaikovsky’s letter scene enlarges a private act of writing into an extended sequence of orchestral anticipation, hesitation and release. pushkin presents the letter as a translation from tatyana’s french; the opera gives it directly to her singing voice. the original is available in the russian text of the passage.

title: The Prince Out Hunting Sees the Castle Where the Princess Lies Sleeping
k: the prince out hunting sees the castle where the princess lies sleeping leon bakst · 1913–22 pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky shared context one of bakst’s seven paintings on the sleeping beauty story, commissioned as a mural cycle for james de rothschild. it is separate from petipa’s 1890 production. bakst also designed diaghilev’s london staging of tchaikovsky’s ballet in 1921: the same artist carried the fairy tale between domestic decoration and the modern stage.

title: Romeo and Juliet, Act II, scene 2
k: romeo and juliet, act ii, scene 2 william shakespeare · c. 1595 pyotr ilyich tchaikovsky documented use balakirev’s proposed subject allowed tchaikovsky to contrast the feud’s agitated sonata material with a love theme first presented by cor anglais and muted violas. shakespeare’s change from public conflict to an intimately observed voice has a musical counterpart in that change of texture.

title: Water Gnome (Vodník)
k: water gnome (vodnik) hanus schwaiger · 1886 antonin dvorak shared context schwaiger’s water creature belongs to the same czech folkloric vocabulary as erben’s ballad and dvorak’s 1896 symphonic poem; a direct source relationship is undocumented. the figure gives bodily form to a being whose musical identity dvorak establishes through a recurrent, sharply articulated orchestral motive. the national gallery’s record dates the painting a decade before the score.

title: Vodník (The Water Goblin) — opening
k: vodnik (the water goblin) — opening karel jaromir erben · 1853 antonin dvorak documented use the harmless domestic labour precedes abduction and a child’s death. dvorak’s symphonic poem follows the ballad’s events closely enough for recurrent musical figures to acquire narrative functions. the opening’s short repeated phrases show why the poem offers a composer rhythmic material as well as a plot. text: oxford’s czech and slovak resources on kytice.

title: The Song of Hiawatha — the wedding dance
k: the song of hiawatha — the wedding dance henry wadsworth longfellow · 1855 antonin dvorak documented use dvorak identified the feast and dancing in hiawatha as a stimulus for the ninth symphony’s scherzo in his december 1893 new york herald interview. longfellow’s poem is a nineteenth-century literary construction using indigenous materials. the dvorak catalogue’s discussion distinguishes the documented scherzo connection from less securely attested claims about the largo.

title: The Swan Princess
k: the swan princess mikhail vrubel · 1900 nikolai rimsky-korsakov shared context vrubel worked on the visual world of the tale of tsar saltan; his wife, nadezhda zabela-vrubel, created the swan princess in mamontov’s production. the painting grew from that theatrical collaboration. its feathered costume, jewelled headdress and uncertain border between body and plumage have a direct counterpart in an opera where transformation is an event in harmony as well as plot.

title: Illustration to Pushkin’s The Golden Cockerel
k: illustration to pushkin’s the golden cockerel ivan bilibin · 1907 nikolai rimsky-korsakov shared context bilibin’s illustrated edition appeared while rimsky-korsakov was completing his opera on the same pushkin tale. this image belongs to the book. bilibin subsequently designed for the opera’s first productions; his bounded colour areas and ornamental borders offered a visual language for the apparently archaic world in which the political satire could operate.

title: The Golden Cockerel — final couplet
k: the golden cockerel — final couplet alexander pushkin · 1834; published 1835 nikolai rimsky-korsakov documented use pushkin ends by refusing to name the lesson. rimsky-korsakov and his librettist vladimir belsky retained the distance between an improbable fairy story and its recognisable human arrangements: the ruler’s promises, his dependence on military advice, and the cost of treating others as possessions. the opera’s framing astrologer makes the status of the spectacle itself unstable.

title: Gabriel Fauré
k: gabriel faure john singer sargent · 1889 gabriel faure documented encounter sargent was a pianist as well as a painter, knew faure personally and helped introduce his music to english musical circles. this portrait records their working friendship. the dark suit and almost unpainted background concentrate attention on the head: compare the social setting of faure’s songs with the density of the musical argument they accommodated.

title: Mezzetin
k: mezzetin antoine watteau · c. 1718–20 gabriel faure shared context mezzetin, a stock lover of the commedia dell’arte, sings to a guitar in a park while a marble woman turns her back on him. this is the world verlaine took from watteau for fetes galantes (1869): the “masques et bergamasques, jouant du luth” of clair de lune, which faure set in 1887 (op. 46 no. 2) with a minuet in the piano that carries on regardless of the voice. the link runs through the poem’s ancestry; a direct source for the song remains undocumented.

title: Clair de lune
sub: Paul Verlaine · 1869; set by Fauré in 1887
k: clair de lune paul verlaine · 1869; set by faure in 1887 gabriel faure documented use faure’s setting, op. 46 no. 2, begins with a piano introduction long enough to establish the dance before the singer enters. debussy set the same poem twice and later used its title for a piano piece. the text names the minor mode; its central contradiction lies between an enacted happiness and the dancers’ disbelief.

title: Poster for the Moravian Teachers’ Choir
k: poster for the moravian teachers’ choir alfons mucha · 1911 leos janacek shared context mucha’s woman in moravian dress listens to a bird. the poster advertises the moravian teachers’ choir, a male-voice ensemble under ferdinand vach and an important interpreter of janacek’s demanding choral music. folk culture, organised amateur singing and contemporary composition meet in this institution. the mucha foundation’s catalogue identifies the costume with the kyjov region.

title: Illustration for the ninth instalment of Liška Bystrouška
k: illustration for the ninth instalment of liska bystrouska stanislav lolek · 16 april 1920 leos janacek documented use lolek’s drawings prompted rudolf tesnohlidek’s newspaper narrative, which in turn supplied janacek with the cunning little vixen. the composer changed the narrative and its ending, placing the forester’s recognition of recurring life after the vixen’s death. the printed drawing preserves the comic, observed animal world from which that operatic structure grew.

title: Near the Malvern Hills
sub: John Joseph Barker · Nineteenth century; undated
k: near the malvern hills john joseph barker · nineteenth century; undated edward elgar shared context the malvern ridge belongs to elgar’s working geography: he lived at malvern link during the years leading to enigma, walked in the hills and later cycled through worcestershire. barker’s painting shares that terrain, with no documented connection to a particular composition. its cultivated foreground recalls the inhabited countryside on which elgar’s musical life depended: nearby households, churches, schools and amateur players.

title: The Dream of Gerontius — the Angel’s farewell
k: the dream of gerontius — the angel’s farewell john henry newman · 1865 edward elgar documented use these are the opening two stanzas of the angel’s final song: the water is purgatory, and the separation is temporary. elgar sets the farewell in d major, with the mezzo-soprano’s line supported by a restrained orchestral texture. the poem’s repeated actions — holding, lowering, releasing — give the final scene its measured pace. newman’s text supplies the theological detail that concert extracts often lose.

title: The Latin Quarter: set design for La bohème, Act II
k: the latin quarter: set design for la boheme, act ii adolfo hohenstein · 1896 giacomo puccini documented use hohenstein designed the setting for the first production at turin’s teatro regio on 1 february 1896. the crowded square is part of the composition’s working apparatus: cafe tables, street traffic, vendors and a passing military band must be visible or audible in relation to one another. puccini’s separate musical groups inhabit the spaces that the designer provides.

title: Scènes de la vie de bohème — preface
k: scenes de la vie de boheme — preface henry murger · 1851 giacomo puccini documented use murger names three possible destinations, only one of them success. puccini’s librettists compressed characters and incidents from the stories and their theatrical adaptation. the final act makes the hospital-and-morgue possibilities concrete, giving the preface’s satire a tragic weight. the original preface sets out the stakes of “bohemian” life.

title: Wie die Thiere den Jäger begraben (How the Animals Bury the Hunter)
k: wie die thiere den jager begraben (how the animals bury the hunter) moritz von schwind · 1850 gustav mahler shared context a children’s picture-sheet from munich: hares carry banners, a fox weeps, deer and boars follow the coffin of the hunter who used to shoot them. mahler cited this kind of image — an old austrian nursery print — as the seed of the funeral march in the first symphony. it explains the movement’s tone exactly: a procession that is both mournful and absurd, with a klezmer-like band (oboes, e♭ clarinets, bass drum with cymbal attached) breaking in on the solemnity.

title: Beethoven Frieze: This Kiss to the Whole World
k: beethoven frieze: this kiss to the whole world gustav klimt · 1902 gustav mahler shared context klimt painted the frieze for the vienna secession’s 1902 exhibition in honour of beethoven, as a visual reading of the ninth symphony’s finale; its last panel takes its title from schiller’s ode to joy. at the opening, mahler conducted his own arrangement of a passage from that finale for wind instruments. the armoured knight on the frieze’s long wall has often been said to carry mahler’s features — an attribution that cannot be proved, but tells you how vienna saw its opera director.

title: Attersee
k: attersee gustav klimt · 1900 gustav mahler shared context the lake where mahler built his first composing hut, at steinbach, and wrote the second and third symphonies (1893–96). klimt summered there from 1900 and painted it on square canvases, cropping the horizon almost out of the picture until the water becomes a field of colour. when the conductor bruno walter visited steinbach and stared at the mountains, mahler told him not to bother: “i have already composed all that.”

title: Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen
sub: Friedrich Rückert · c. 1821; set by Mahler 1901
k: ich bin der welt abhanden gekommen friedrich ruckert · c. 1821; set by mahler 1901 gustav mahler documented use the middle stanza is omitted here. mahler set the poem in f major for voice and a reduced orchestra, with the cor anglais carrying a line that seems to grow out of the voice. he said of it: “it is my very self.” the adagietto of the fifth symphony, composed the same summer, is in the same key and breathes the same air.

title: Der Abschied — closing lines
k: der abschied — closing lines gustav mahler, after hans bethge · 1908 gustav mahler documented use bethge’s die chinesische flote (1907) gave mahler loose german paraphrases of tang poets — li bai, wang wei, meng haoran — already filtered through french and german translations. for the end of der abschied mahler stopped adapting and wrote these lines himself.

title: Under the Wave off Kanagawa
k: under the wave off kanagawa katsushika hokusai · c. 1830–32 claude debussy documented use debussy chose an adaptation of hokusai’s wave for the cover of durand’s 1905 edition of la mer. the printed score isolates and stylises the wave from the view shown here. the score’s subtitle remains ‘three symphonic sketches’.

title: Nocturne: Blue and Silver — Chelsea
k: nocturne: blue and silver — chelsea james mcneill whistler · 1871 claude debussy shared context whistler’s series of painted nocturnes supplied debussy with a model for the title of his orchestral triptych. whistler had borrowed a musical genre-name to direct attention towards arrangements of colour; debussy took it back with that pictorial implication. this thames view represents the series.

title: L’Après-midi d’un faune — opening
k: l’apres-midi d’un faune — opening stephane mallarme · 1876 claude debussy documented use the faun’s memory blurs encounter and invention. in debussy’s prelude, the returning flute phrase acquires changing harmonic contexts. mallarme attended the 1894 premiere and wrote his approval to debussy afterwards. the excerpt preserves the opening’s interrupted syntax.

title: Impression, soleil levant
k: impression, soleil levant claude monet · 1872 claude debussy editorial comparison the title of monet’s le havre harbour painting helped give impressionism its name after the 1874 exhibition. debussy was repeatedly placed under that label. compare the few dark boats that establish distance against the harbour’s coloured marks with the separation of rhythmic layers in la mer.

title: Also sprach Zarathustra — Zarathustra’s prologue, §1
k: also sprach zarathustra — zarathustra’s prologue, §1 friedrich nietzsche · 1883 richard strauss documented use zarathustra addresses the sun before descending from his mountain solitude. strauss’s orchestral sunrise makes the address audible; later section headings draw on other chapters. nietzsche’s metaphor gives a reason for the opening’s direction, from a low pedal to a high brass declaration. the german text supplies the source.

title: Judith II (Salome)
k: judith ii (salome) gustav klimt · 1909 richard strauss shared context the painting’s alternative title records the period’s tendency to confuse judith, who kills holofernes, with salome, who demands jochanaan’s head. strauss’s opera concerns the latter. both belong to the same early-twentieth-century reconsideration of the biblical woman holding a severed male head. the date also coincides with elektra: classical and biblical subjects were being detached from reassuring academic conventions.

title: Der Rosenkavalier — the Marschallin on time
k: der rosenkavalier — the marschallin on time hugo von hofmannsthal · 1911 richard strauss documented use the act i speech is written for a woman who understands that her young lover will leave her. strauss largely withdraws the conversational bustle around the marschallin, giving her words room within an orchestral continuity that does not stop. hofmannsthal turns the passing of time into the comedy’s subject; the final trio will make her act upon the knowledge expressed here. the german libretto preserves the speech in its theatrical context.

title: Lemminkäinen’s Mother
k: lemminkainen’s mother akseli gallen-kallela · 1897 jean sibelius shared context in the kalevala, lemminkainen is killed during his attempt to shoot the swan of tuonela; his mother gathers the dismembered body and restores him to life. gallen-kallela paints the body beside the river, with the swan in the distance. sibelius’s lemminkainen in tuonela treats the same narrative world. the picture postdates the legends’ first performance; a shared text and an artistic friendship connect the works.

title: Symposium
k: symposium akseli gallen-kallela · 1894 jean sibelius shared context from left to right: gallen-kallela, oskar merikanto, robert kajanus and sibelius. the group met in helsinki, notably at the hotel kamp, and discussed music and the other arts. kajanus’s practical advocacy mattered as much as the conversation: he conducted sibelius’s works and later recorded several symphonies. the painting places the composer within a sociable, metropolitan artistic circle.

title: Kullervo Cursing
k: kullervo cursing akseli gallen-kallela · 1899 jean sibelius shared context kullervo raises his fist after breaking his inherited knife on a stone baked into his bread. this episode precedes the incest and suicide central to sibelius’s five-movement work. the painting supplies narrative context. both artists shape the kalevala into modern works with individual formal decisions.

title: Portrait d’Erik Satie
k: portrait d’erik satie suzanne valadon · 1893 erik satie documented encounter valadon painted satie during their brief relationship in montmartre. her outline fixes the head and narrow torso against a plain background, without a piano or other professional attribute. the picture records a relationship between two working artists. she died in 1938, and the painting is in the public domain.

title: Le Pauvre pêcheur
k: le pauvre pecheur pierre puvis de chavannes · 1881 erik satie editorial comparison satie admired puvis de chavannes; the painter’s restricted colour, flattened space and restrained gestures provide an artistic context for his preference for reduced means. the link is to the painter’s work generally; this canvas is not named in the score of socrate. compare the separation of its figures and their restrained gestures with the work’s detached narration of socrates’s death.

title: Prometheus
k: prometheus jean delville · 1907 alexander scriabin shared context delville’s prometheus belongs to the belgian painter’s symbolist and theosophical interpretation of the myth: fire becomes an emblem of intellectual and spiritual illumination. scriabin knew delville, who designed the published score of prometheus. a shared intellectual circle and a documented collaboration connect the two artists.

title: Cover design for Prometheus: The Poem of Fire
k: cover design for prometheus: the poem of fire jean delville · 1911 alexander scriabin documented use the printed design places the score inside the same esoteric visual culture as delville’s painting. separate documents record the colour correspondences of the clavier a lumieres. scriabin’s system orders hues partly through the circle of fifths, while the score’s two light lines distinguish local harmonic change from larger formal spans. gawboy and townsend’s study compares sabaneev’s 1911 table with scriabin’s own 1913 annotations.

title: Die Toteninsel (Isle of the Dead), first version
k: die toteninsel (isle of the dead), first version arnold bocklin · 1880 sergei rachmaninoff shared context a boat bearing a white figure and coffin approaches rock, cypresses and openings cut into the island. bocklin made five versions between 1880 and 1886; this is the first, in basel. rachmaninoff encountered the image through a black-and-white reproduction in paris in 1907; which version it reproduced remains uncertain. his 1909 symphonic poem translates the approach into a repeated 5/8 figure.

title: Rachmaninoff with family and friends at Ivanovka
k: rachmaninoff with family and friends at ivanovka unidentified photographer · mid-1890s sergei rachmaninoff shared context rachmaninoff stands second from the left in the back row. this is the satin family’s estate near tambov, where he first spent a summer in 1890 and returned to compose before 1917. the photograph places the music within the household where he worked. ivanovka provided the working conditions for the first concerto and much of the third; it was also a farm on which he spent substantial earnings.

title: Portrait of Sergei Rachmaninoff
k: portrait of sergei rachmaninoff konstantin somov · 1925 sergei rachmaninoff shared context somov, a member of the mir iskusstva circle, painted rachmaninoff during his own years abroad. the frontal head, dark coat and restrained background present the professional musician without a piano or score. its date falls between the establishment of rachmaninoff’s american touring career and his return to major composition with the fourth concerto in 1926.

title: The Bells — opening section
k: the bells — opening section edgar allan poe · 1849 sergei rachmaninoff documented use rachmaninoff set konstantin balmont’s russian adaptation of poe’s english in op. 35. the four-part sequence remains, from these sleigh bells through wedding and alarm bells to the iron funeral bell. repeated words already behave as rhythmic cells; rachmaninoff gives repetition to the chorus and orchestral accompaniment as well as the soloist. the complete poem was published in 1849, after poe’s death.

title: Не пой, красавица, при мне… (Do not sing, beautiful one, before me)
k: не пои, красавица, при мне... (do not sing, beautiful one, before me) alexander pushkin · 1828; set by rachmaninoff 1892 sergei rachmaninoff documented use the first two of four stanzas. rachmaninoff set the complete poem as op. 4 no. 4, in a minor, and dedicated the song to natalia satina. the piano’s introduction establishes the returning music before the singer asks not to hear it: memory has already entered the room. the poem predates rachmaninoff’s exile by almost ninety years, and his setting by twenty-five.

title: Snap the Whip
k: snap the whip winslow homer · 1872 charles ives editorial comparison homer’s boys play a chain game outside a rural schoolhouse in the years after the civil war. ives’s childhood in danbury supplied comparable games, parades and community music-making for later scores, including the child’s outing in putnam’s camp. the link is shared subject matter; there is no evidence ives used this painting as a source. homer’s strained line of connected bodies offers a visual counterpart to coordinated activity that threatens to pull apart.

title: Self-Reliance — excerpt
k: self-reliance — excerpt ralph waldo emerson · 1841 charles ives shared context the opening movement of the concord sonata is named for emerson, and ives discusses his writing at length in essays before a sonata. ives’s themes interrupt and qualify one another, as arguments do in the essays, finding continuity in their exchanges. this is prose, line-broken here for reading.

title: Walden, “Sounds” — excerpt
k: walden, “sounds” — excerpt henry david thoreau · 1854 charles ives shared context the concord sonata’s last movement concerns thoreau at walden and includes an optional flute, the instrument thoreau himself played. this passage compares mechanical and natural sound while keeping their sources distinct. ives similarly lets a church bell, hymn or march retain its character within an outdoor setting. the excerpt is prose.

title: Blue Self-Portrait
k: blue self-portrait arnold schoenberg · 1910 arnold schoenberg documented encounter schoenberg painted this small frontal self-portrait during the period of op. 11 and erwartung. colour alters the face without eliminating it: the blue surface is still organised around eyes, nose and mouth. his first exhibition took place in vienna in 1910, and four paintings appeared in the first blaue reiter exhibition in 1911. commons identifies this reproduction as public domain; schoenberg’s works entered the public domain in life-plus-seventy-year jurisdictions in 2022.

title: The Schoenberg Family
k: the schoenberg family richard gerstl · 1908 arnold schoenberg documented encounter gerstl painted arnold, mathilde and their children during his association with the family. broad brushmarks break up the conventional portrait group; the figures remain present without precise facial description. his affair with mathilde and his suicide in november 1908 coincide with the second string quartet’s completion and first performance. the connection is biographical.

title: Composition V
k: composition v wassily kandinsky · 1911 arnold schoenberg shared context kandinsky began corresponding with schoenberg after a munich concert in january 1911. this large canvas was exhibited with the first blaue reiter exhibition, where schoenberg’s paintings also appeared. its residual last judgement imagery is broken into lines and colour masses. the parallel lies in the pair’s debate about inherited artistic rules.

title: Mondestrunken
sub: Albert Giraud, German version by Otto Erich Hartleben · French original 1884; German version 1892
k: mondestrunken albert giraud, german version by otto erich hartleben · french original 1884; german version 1892 arnold schoenberg documented use the first two stanzas of the opening poem in pierrot lunaire. hartleben’s german freely reworks giraud. the repeated opening lines belong to the poem’s rondel construction; schoenberg varies their musical setting. verbal recurrence and musical variation are deliberately separated.

title: Set design for Act I of Daphnis et Chloé
k: set design for act i of daphnis et chloe leon bakst · 1912 maurice ravel documented use bakst designed the scenery and costumes for the ballets russes production of ravel’s ballet, choreographed by fokine and first performed in paris in june 1912. the drawing’s antiquity is a stage construction: monumental landscape surrounds the space in which human figures move. ravel’s wordless chorus and slowly accumulated orchestral layers create a corresponding scale. harvard identifies this sheet as act i.

title: Ondine — opening and closing paragraphs
sub: Aloysius Bertrand · 1842; text from the 1895 edition
k: ondine — opening and closing paragraphs aloysius bertrand · 1842; text from the 1895 edition maurice ravel documented use the intervening paragraphs, in which ondine describes her underwater palace and proposes marriage, are omitted. bertrand’s gaspard de la nuit was published posthumously in 1842; ravel’s 1908 piano triptych prints its three source poems. the first movement must distinguish the water’s continuous motion from the spirit’s song, then accommodate her laughter and disappearance. the french follows the 1895 mercure de france edition; the translation here is our own.

title: Le Petit Poucet: the children at the ogre’s door
k: le petit poucet: the children at the ogre’s door gustave dore · 1867 edition maurice ravel shared context the lantern isolates seven children beneath the ogre’s house; the architectural scale makes their physical vulnerability measurable. ravel’s petit poucet, the second piece of ma mere l’oye, uses the same perrault tale but an earlier incident: the lost breadcrumb trail. wandering lines and changing bar lengths replace a secure processional pulse; birds enter the orchestral version as instrumental calls. the link with dore is the shared text.

title: Court Ball in Vienna
k: court ball in vienna wilhelm gause · 1900 maurice ravel shared context ravel planned a homage to johann strauss as early as 1906, provisionally titled wien; he finished it after the war, in 1919–20, as la valse. gause’s view of a habsburg court ball — chandeliers, uniforms, a floor packed with turning couples — is the scene the score’s preface names. what ravel did to it is the point: the waltz is assembled from fragments emerging out of murk in the double basses, built to a brilliant climax, and then driven past it until the three-beat metre breaks apart.

title: Preface to the score of La Valse
k: preface to the score of la valse maurice ravel · 1920 maurice ravel documented use ravel printed this scenario at the head of the score of his “poeme choregraphique”. it is also a set of orchestration instructions in disguise: the clouds are the muted, divided double basses that open the piece; the gaps are the first waltz fragments surfacing in the bassoons; “eclate au ff” marks the exact dynamic at which the full orchestra arrives. ravel insisted the setting was 1855, not 1914 — but the score’s violent ending has been heard as an epitaph for that court ever since.

title: Bartók recording Slovak folk songs at Zobordarázs
k: bartok recording slovak folk songs at zobordarazs photographer unidentified · 1907 bela bartok shared context the phonograph horn makes the act of collection visible: a particular singer performs for a recording machine while other villagers gather nearby. zobordarazs is now drazovce, slovakia. the bartok archives dates this photograph to 1907, rather than the 1908 supplied in the commons metadata. pair it with the slovak volumes of for children: the compositional source is a performed and variable melody.

title: Bartók during his first Transylvanian collecting trip
k: bartok during his first transylvanian collecting trip istvan kovats · 1907 bela bartok shared context kovats photographed bartok at gyergyoszentmiklos, now gheorgheni, during the collecting expedition of 1907. this identification follows the archive’s 2022 exhibition catalogue, rather than commons’ approximate 1903 date. the trip’s pentatonic hungarian songs belong to the documented background of the stylistic change around the fourteen bagatelles and first quartet.

title: The Lonely Cedar
k: the lonely cedar tivadar csontvary kosztka · 1907 bela bartok editorial comparison csontvary, who died in 1919, painted a lebanese cedar. the hungarian painter’s foreign subject shows the reach of his material beyond his own country. beside bartok’s night music, the isolated branching form and broad background offer a comparison of foreground and field. the pairing is visual, with no claim of musical influence. the national gallery catalogue records the canvas and its date.

title: Ruins of the Greek Theatre at Taormina
k: ruins of the greek theatre at taormina tivadar csontvary kosztka · 1904–05 bela bartok editorial comparison the theatre’s masonry establishes a close, articulated foreground against sea, coast and mountain. paired with music for strings, percussion and celesta, it invites comparison between a large design and the separate planes through which that design becomes perceptible. csontvary was an older hungarian contemporary working outside academic naturalism; the link here is formal, with no documented connection to the score.

title: Kiss to the Earth: second variant of the scenery design for The Rite of Spring
k: kiss to the earth: second variant of the scenery design for the rite of spring nicholas roerich · 1912 igor stravinsky documented use roerich was the ballet’s co-author as well as its designer. this study belongs to the 1913 production’s first part, “adoration of the earth”; its receding hills and stones place collective action in a landscape. the scenario’s games, processions and sacrifice supplied occasions for contrasted musical blocks. roerich’s archaeological interests informed these modern constructions of pagan ceremony. commons identifies this pre-1931 design as public domain; roerich died in 1947.

title: Costume design for The Firebird
k: costume design for the firebird leon bakst · 1910 igor stravinsky documented use bakst’s design belongs to the ballets russes production that introduced stravinsky to paris. its elaborated wings and plumage made the supernatural creature visible through a dancer’s body; the score distinguishes that creature through chromatic movement, rapid figuration and orchestral colour. the production was collaborative: fokine choreographed, alexander golovin designed the scenery and other costumes, and karsavina created the firebird.
