title: Tsarevich Ivan and the Firebird
sub: Ivan Bilibin · 1899, dated in the image
k: tsarevich ivan and the firebird ivan bilibin · 1899, dated in the image igor stravinsky shared context bilibin shows ivan catching a feather from the bird among the apple trees, a scene from the tale of ivan tsarevich, the firebird and the grey wolf. the ballet’s scenario combines material from several russian tales. the illustration establishes the existing visual vocabulary — the bird’s long plumage, the orchard, ivan’s clothing — on which a paris audience’s russian fairy-tale spectacle depended. it belongs to the source tradition, outside the designs for the 1910 production.

title: A Rake’s Progress, Plate VIII: In Bedlam
k: a rake’s progress, plate viii: in bedlam william hogarth · 1735 igor stravinsky documented use stravinsky saw hogarth’s series in chicago in 1947 and proposed it as an opera subject. this final plate supplies the destination, bedlam; auden and kallman added nick shadow and the pact with the devil. hogarth’s sequential scenes find a musical counterpart in the opera’s separate arias, ensembles and recitatives. the closing epilogue, delivered outside the action, restores the moral address to an audience that the prints make through their captions and details.

title: Nature, central panel of the Alpine Triptych
k: nature, central panel of the alpine triptych giovanni segantini · 1897–99 anton webern documented use webern’s plan for his unnumbered string quartet of 1905 refers to segantini’s triptych, whose panels were known to him as werden, sein and vergehen — becoming, being and passing away. this central panel places cattle and figures within the engadine mountains at sunset. the documented connection belongs to that early work’s conception.

title: Abendland II
sub: Georg Trakl · Published in Sebastian im Traum, 1915; set by Webern 1919
k: abendland ii georg trakl · published in sebastian im traum, 1915; set by webern 1919 anton webern documented use webern set this as the third of the six songs, op. 14, for voice, clarinet, violin and cello. trakl’s clauses move from homeland to ruined wall, vineyard and eagles, leaving the connections unstated. the score gives those transitions space through sparse instrumental entries. the german is the version used in the song; the english here is a new translation.

title: Portrait of Alban Berg
k: portrait of alban berg arnold schoenberg · 1910 alban berg documented encounter schoenberg painted his pupil in the year of the string quartet, op. 3. the tall, narrow canvas belongs to the teacher’s concentrated period of portrait painting; it depicts a working relationship that began with harmony lessons in 1904 and continued after berg’s operatic success.

title: De profundis clamavi — opening quatrain
sub: Charles Baudelaire · 1857; text from the 1861 edition
k: de profundis clamavi — opening quatrain charles baudelaire · 1857; text from the 1861 edition alban berg documented use the finale of the lyric suite conceals a setting of this poem in stefan george’s german translation. berg’s annotated copy for hanna fuchs-robettin supplied the evidence discovered by george perle in 1977. the french original appears here. its address to one absent beloved explains the vocal conception behind the instrumental lament.

title: Romeo and Juliet
k: romeo and juliet frank dicksee · 1884 sergei prokofiev shared context dicksee and prokofiev work from the same shakespeare play. the painting concentrates the lovers’ encounter into an embrace on the balcony; the ballet gives the encounter a sequence of approaches, withdrawals and sustained phrases. compare the image with the end of act i. the contrast between the private meeting and the capulets’ public ceremonial behaviour, heard in the knights’ dance usually detached from the score, is already built into shakespeare’s arrangement of scenes.

title: Fix Bayonets! Hurrah! Hurrah! (The Attack)
k: fix bayonets! hurrah! hurrah! (the attack) vasily vereshchagin · 1887–95 sergei prokofiev shared context one of vereshchagin’s napoleon i in russia paintings, dealing with the same 1812 campaign that occupies the war scenes of prokofiev’s opera. the advancing soldiers fill the foreground, bringing the viewer into the movement of bodies. the link is the campaign; use of the canvas as a source is undocumented. set it beside the opera’s borodino scene and tolstoy’s insistence that no general can encompass a battle’s simultaneous actions.

title: Cinderella
k: cinderella gustave dore · 1867 edition sergei prokofiev shared context dore’s illustration belongs to an edition of perrault’s tales; nikolai volkov also used perrault for the scenario of prokofiev’s cinderella. the shared source matters because the fairy’s transformation, the ball and the time limit require different kinds of stage time. prokofiev gives each a musical mechanism: changes of orchestral colour for transformation, extended dances for the ball, and repeated clock figures for the limit.

title: Idols, sketch
k: idols, sketch nicholas roerich · 1901 sergei prokofiev shared context roerich’s fenced sanctuary belongs to his imagined ancient rus. he later devised the scenario and designs for stravinsky’s the rite of spring; diaghilev’s subsequent prehistoric commission to prokofiev produced ala and lolli and, after its rejection, the scythian suite. the link is the ballets russes interest in a reconstructed pagan past. roerich’s repeated posts and carved figures offer a visual counterpart to the suite’s blocks of repeated rhythm.

title: War and Peace: Natasha at the window
sub: Leo Tolstoy · 1865–69; Volume II, Part III, Chapter II
k: war and peace: natasha at the window leo tolstoy · 1865–69; volume ii, part iii, chapter ii sergei prokofiev documented use prince andrei hears this conversation without the women knowing he is below their window. prokofiev and mira mendelson made the otradnoye episode the opera’s opening scene: natasha’s delight reaches a listener within the drama before it reaches us as an operatic declaration. the extract gives tolstoy’s prose, with paragraphing from the russian virtual library text.

title: Lili and Nadia Boulanger
k: lili and nadia boulanger agence meurisse · 1913 lili boulanger shared context the photograph belongs to the press coverage surrounding lili’s prix de rome. it places the sisters in the same documentary frame before nadia’s long teaching career made her the better-known name. their musical collaboration was practical: study, performance, copying and, at the end of lili’s life, dictation. the surviving scores distinguish two composing careers.

title: Elle était descendue
sub: Francis Jammes · From Tristesses, 1906; set in 1913–14
k: elle etait descendue francis jammes · from tristesses, 1906; set in 1913–14 lili boulanger documented use the first song of clairieres dans le ciel begins with this precise memory: wet plants, an awkward movement, a gaze. jammes describes the meadow twice as the speaker returns to it. boulanger’s cycle similarly allows remembered musical material to return with altered significance. jammes died in 1938; this is the public-domain french original with a new translation.

title: Le Groupe des Six
k: le groupe des six jacques-emile blanche · 1922 francis poulenc shared context blanche’s portrait of the circle includes the pianist marcelle meyer and jean cocteau as well as composers. it records a network of performers, writers and friends. poulenc’s study with koechlin supplied private technical discipline behind that sociable public image.

title: Le Dromadaire, from Le Bestiaire
k: le dromadaire, from le bestiaire raoul dufy · 1911 francis poulenc shared context apollinaire’s poems were published with dufy’s woodcuts before poulenc selected six of them in 1919. the book joins animal image and compressed verbal form. compare the print’s bounded black-and-white shapes with the song’s short phrases: both work at a scale that makes every addition conspicuous.

title: Le Dromadaire
sub: Guillaume Apollinaire · 1911; set by Poulenc in 1919
k: le dromadaire guillaume apollinaire · 1911; set by poulenc in 1919 francis poulenc documented use the first of poulenc’s six bestiaire songs retains the poem’s disproportionately grand traveller and its modest conditional ending within the compass of apollinaire’s five lines. he died in 1918, and the 1911 original is public domain; the english translation here is new.

title: Portrait of Mitya Shostakovich
k: portrait of mitya shostakovich boris kustodiev · 1919 dmitri shostakovich documented encounter kustodiev drew shostakovich in the year he entered the petrograd conservatory and inscribed the portrait to his young friend. the memorial apartment’s catalogue distinguishes this 1919 drawing from a second portrait made at gaspra in 1923; the reproduced commons file is the earlier work. it documents an actual connection with the painter, before the first symphony made the student an internationally performed composer.

title: Anti-aircraft guns near St Isaac’s Cathedral, Leningrad
k: anti-aircraft guns near st isaac’s cathedral, leningrad boris kudoyarov · 24 november 1941 dmitri shostakovich shared context kudoyarov photographed an anti-aircraft battery firing beside st isaac’s during the siege. shostakovich had already been evacuated and was completing the seventh symphony in kuibyshev; the picture records the city to which he dedicated it. the symphony was performed inside leningrad on 9 august 1942. commons identifies this file as public domain under its russian archival-rights declaration.

title: The Nose — the nose refuses its owner
k: the nose — the nose refuses its owner nikolai gogol · 1836 dmitri shostakovich documented use in the cathedral encounter, kovalyov’s nose defeats his claim through the language of official rank and departmental boundaries. shostakovich’s opera preserves that collision between an impossible event and exact bureaucratic procedure, giving the nose a tenor voice and kovalyov a baritone. the extract follows the russian text in the academy of sciences collected edition; the english translation is ours. leskov provides the separate source for lady macbeth of the mtsensk district.

title: Wood Thrush, plate 73 of The Birds of America
sub: Robert Havell after John James Audubon · 1829
k: wood thrush, plate 73 of the birds of america robert havell after john james audubon · 1829 olivier messiaen shared context the wood thrush, hylocichla mustelina, is messiaen’s grive des bois. it supplies the title and musical material of movement ten of des canyons aux etoiles.... the work’s commentary describes its clear major arpeggio and lower rustling aftermath. havell’s plate after audubon identifies the same bird visually, beside flowering dogwood. the pairing rests on the shared species. the nineteenth-century artwork is public domain; the national gallery’s scan is released under cc0.

title: The Mocking Bird, plate 21 of The Birds of America
sub: Robert Havell after John James Audubon · 1827
k: the mocking bird, plate 21 of the birds of america robert havell after john james audubon · 1827 olivier messiaen shared context movement nine of des canyons aux etoiles..., le moqueur polyglotte, gives the northern mockingbird an unaccompanied piano movement. short calls, trills and repeated-note figures make one instrument carry a changing repertory of gestures. audubon’s birds confront a snake at their nest. the connection is the identified species and the act of detailed observation. like the wood-thrush plate, this public-domain engraving is available as a cc0 national gallery scan.

title: Revelation 10:1, 5–6 — the angel’s oath
sub: John of Patmos; Latin Vulgate tradition · First century CE; Clementine Vulgate edition, 1598
k: revelation 10:1, 5–6 — the angel’s oath john of patmos; latin vulgate tradition · first century ce; clementine vulgate edition, 1598 olivier messiaen documented use the angel, rainbow and oath in this biblical source supply the quartet’s programme. verses 2–4 are omitted, with the break shown above; the latin follows the public-domain clementine vulgate. ‘no more time’ translates the wording literally and follows messiaen’s musical reading of it; the passage is also understood as announcing no further delay before fulfilment. slow louanges and rhythmic palindromes make that interpretation audible without a sung text.

title: Judith and Job window, Sainte-Chapelle
sub: Thirteenth-century Parisian glass painters; photograph by Yair Haklai · c. 1248, with later restorations; photographed 12 April 2017
k: judith and job window, sainte-chapelle thirteenth-century parisian glass painters; photograph by yair haklai · c. 1248, with later restorations; photographed 12 april 2017 olivier messiaen documented encounter messiaen visited the sainte-chapelle as a child and repeatedly connected its coloured light with his musical thinking. et exspecto resurrectionem mortuorum received its first performance here on 7 may 1965 under serge baudo. this photograph shows the judith and job bay within the chapel’s medieval biblical glazing. the image is by yair haklai, licensed cc by-sa 4.0. medieval glass and later restoration coexist in the present window.

title: The Borough, Letter XXII — Peter Grimes
k: the borough, letter xxii — peter grimes george crabbe · 1810 benjamin britten documented use crabbe was born in aldeburgh in 1754. these six lines describe grimes seeking out the estuary after the deaths of his apprentices; spelling is modernised. the poem supplies the opera’s subject. slater and britten shift its moral balance, giving grimes a capacity for imagination that crabbe’s sustained account of abuse scarcely permits. the water is already described through sound — a restricted, repetitive stream.

title: Anthem for Doomed Youth
k: anthem for doomed youth wilfred owen · 1917; published 1920 benjamin britten documented use britten places this sonnet in the opening movement of the war requiem, giving it to the tenor and chamber orchestra. owen’s substitution of guns for bells and shells for a choir confronts the actual choir singing the requiem around him. the poem’s refusal of adequate funeral ritual interrupts the ritual being performed.

title: Golding Constable’s Kitchen Garden
k: golding constable’s kitchen garden john constable · c. 1815 benjamin britten shared context constable paints the cultivated land behind his father’s house at east bergholt in suffolk. the connection is regional; there is no documented influence. britten’s aldeburgh music likewise belongs to a working county of gardens, churches, farms and fishing boats. read the ordered plots against crabbe’s estuary: both show a countryside shaped by human labour.

title: The Triumph of Death
k: the triumph of death pieter bruegel the elder · c. 1562 gyorgy ligeti editorial comparison le grand macabre takes place in breughelland, the name inherited from michel de ghelderode’s play. bruegel’s crowded panorama offers a visual counterpart: soldiers, lovers, clergy and aristocrats occupy the same field while death overrides their distinctions. ligeti’s ending departs from its apparent finality: nekrotzar’s promised annihilation may have failed.

title: Lux aeterna
sub: Latin Requiem liturgy · Traditional Latin text; set by Ligeti in 1966
k: lux aeterna latin requiem liturgy · traditional latin text; set by ligeti in 1966 gyorgy ligeti documented use the communion text of the mass for the dead is the source of ligeti’s sixteen-part motet. its promise of light differs from the judgement imagery dominating his requiem. he repeats and overlaps its words, making individual syllables part of a shifting choral harmony before a whole phrase can be understood.

title: Polyphony
k: polyphony paul klee · 1932 pierre boulez editorial comparison boulez first encountered klee’s work in avignon in 1947 and returned to it in le pays fertile: paul klee (1989). klee’s dots, coloured fields and overlapping divisions make several organisations visible at once. boulez valued his demonstrations of how elementary operations can generate a complex form. the painting’s title names the musical analogy explicitly.

title: Une dentelle s’abolit
k: une dentelle s’abolit stephane mallarme · 1887 pierre boulez documented use this sonnet supplies the text of ‘improvisation ii’, the central movement of pli selon pli. the mandore is a small plucked string instrument; the poem connects its hollow body with an absent bed and a possible birth. boulez stretches syllables and surrounds the soprano with instrumental resonance. the french follows the 1887 printed text; the translation retains its unresolved syntax.

title: Star Ushak Carpet
sub: Unidentified Anatolian weavers · Probably seventeenth century
k: star ushak carpet unidentified anatolian weavers · probably seventeenth century morton feldman editorial comparison feldman collected middle eastern rugs and discussed their unequal repetitions in ‘crippled symmetry’ (1981). this anatolian carpet is not documented as one he owned. its repeating star medallions and bounded field make his comparison tangible: a motif can recur with changes to its intervals, contours or patches of colour. the met’s photograph is released under cc0.

title: Coptic Textile Fragment
sub: Unidentified Egyptian weavers · Late third–fifth century
k: coptic textile fragment unidentified egyptian weavers · late third–fifth century morton feldman editorial comparison in his note for coptic light, feldman identifies ancient textiles at the louvre as a stimulus, asking how fragments can retain the character of the civilisation that made them. this met fragment offers a comparison. its surviving threads and colour boundaries suggest the persistence and renewal of instrumental colour in the orchestral work. the museum image is cc0.

title: Franz Kafka
k: franz kafka unknown photographer · 1923–24 gyorgy kurtag shared context kafka’s diaries, letters and notebooks supply the forty texts of kafka-fragmente. this late portrait belongs to the period before his death in 1924. kurtag’s work repeatedly changes the scale at which the writer is heard: an aphorism lasting seconds may stand beside a much longer scene for the same soprano and violin.

title: Die Guten gehn im gleichen Schritt
sub: Franz Kafka · Early twentieth century; set by Kurtág 1985–87
k: die guten gehn im gleichen schritt franz kafka · early twentieth century; set by kurtag 1985–87 gyorgy kurtag documented use the opening text of kafka-fragmente. its contrast is already musical: common step against surrounding dances. kurtag gives the soprano and violin distinct rhythmic behaviour. line breaks make kafka’s prose legible here.

title: An Zimmern
