title: How can two melodies fit together?
k: how can two melodies fit together? counterpoint: two melodies, one argument how it works independent lines counterpoint regulates the meeting of melodies. each part must make sense horizontally, as a singable line, while its intervals with the other parts make sense vertically. johann joseph fux’s gradus ad parnassum, published in vienna in 1725, teaches that double responsibility through a dialogue between aloysius, representing palestrina, and the pupil josephus. its exercises isolate problems that a composer can practise before managing the rhythmic freedom of an actual motet. speciesthe five stages are note against note; two against one; four against one; tied notes or suspensions; and a mixture of the preceding rhythms, called florid counterpoint. in first species, a new note accompanies each note of a supplied cantus firmus, a fixed melody in long values. the vertical intervals are consonances: unisons, octaves and fifths, together with thirds and sixths. parallel perfect fifths and octaves are excluded because they make two parts behave like one doubled line. parallel thirds and sixths remain available. contrary motion, in which one part rises while another falls, offers a particularly audible way to establish independence. dissonance becomes possible when rhythm explains it. in second species, a weak-beat passing note can bridge two consonances by step. in fourth species, a note is prepared as a consonance, held across a change in the other voice, and resolved down by step: preparation, suspension, resolution. a fourth above the bass counts as dissonant in this discipline, even though the same interval can be acceptable between upper parts in a larger texture. consonance here is a matter of practice and position as well as acoustics. inversion is not reversalinvertible counterpoint exchanges the vertical positions of complete lines. melodic inversion turns upward intervals downward; retrograde reads a sequence backwards. these are different operations. in counterpoint invertible at the octave, thirds become sixths when the lower line is moved above the upper. fifths become fourths: a consonance has become a dissonance, so the original fifth needs special treatment if both arrangements are to work. bach designs subjects and accompanying lines with such exchanges in mind. the two invented examples separate the jobs: the opening example keeps every simultaneous interval consonant; the later one lets the same two lines trade places.

title: What happens when the same tune enters again?
sub: Fugue: an entrance changes the texture
k: what happens when the same tune enters again? fugue: an entrance changes the texture how it works imitation a fugue starts by making a melody identifiable before making it compete with other melodies. one voice states the subject; another enters with an answer, normally at the dominant level. a real answer transposes every interval exactly. a tonal answer adjusts an interval, often exchanging a tonic-to-dominant gesture for dominant-to-tonic, to keep the opening within the home key. the distinction concerns exact and adjusted transposition. one exact subjectthe example is the opening alto line of bach’s c major fugue, bwv 846, from book i of the well-tempered clavier (1722). the subject reaches e on beat three of bar 2; the remaining semiquavers continue the line. the first voice continues when the second begins. if its accompanying material regularly returns against later statements of the subject, that material is a countersubject. a useful countersubject often works above or below the subject, requiring invertible counterpoint. bwv 846 proceeds without a regular countersubject; its initial answer is real, and its four opening entries arrive in the order subject, answer, answer, subject. the opening round of entries is called the exposition. subsequent entries may move into related keys, changing the subject’s harmonic surroundings while preserving enough of its intervals and rhythm for recognition. an episode is a passage without a complete subject statement, often made from a fragment sequenced at successive pitch levels. an episode can move the harmony towards a new entrance or thin the texture after a crowded passage. bwv 846 sustains its argument largely through entries and overlaps. strettoa new statement begins before the previous statement has finished. the distance between entries changes while the tempo can remain steady. in stretto, the subject must combine contrapuntally with a displaced version of itself. bach can shorten the interval between entrances, change their registers, or let more voices join the overlap. those choices produce intensification without introducing a louder dynamic or a new theme. augmentation lengthens the subject’s note values; inversion reverses the direction of its intervals. listen for the moment of each entrance: it may interrupt an episode, complete a cadence, or turn an apparently accompanying voice into the principal speaker.

title: How can numbers tell a player what to play?
sub: Figured bass: numbers above a moving foundation
k: how can numbers tell a player what to play? figured bass: numbers above a moving foundation how it works a working notation figured bass gives a player a written bass line and numbers specifying intervals above it. a harpsichordist, organist or theorbo player usually supplies the upper voices, choosing their spacing, rhythm and register to suit the singers or instrumentalists. in a baroque continuo group, a cello or bassoon may reinforce the bass without playing chords. the division between bass instrument and chordal instrument answers practical needs, and the combination can vary between ensembles. count from the bassover c, a 6 asks for a; over e, a 6 asks for c. the numeral names an interval above whichever bass note is sounding. an unfigured bass commonly implies a third and fifth, adjusted to the key signature and the musical context. a 6 normally abbreviates 6/3; 6/4 asks for a fourth and sixth. over e in c major, g and c therefore produce a first-inversion c major chord. over g, c and e form a six-four sonority. at a cadence those upper notes often move down to b and d over the same g bass: the figures 6–5 and 4–3 describe the movement directly. a bare accidental usually alters the third; an accidental beside a numeral alters that numbered interval. the numbers leave essential decisions open. doubling a note can strengthen a chord, but doubling a leading note may make a clean resolution difficult. a singer’s sustained dissonance needs space in the accompaniment. a slow aria may invite an arpeggiated texture; a rapid recitative requires the player to follow the delivery of the text. realisation is therefore both harmony and counterpoint: the player is composing several lines while accompanying an existing one. figures are not chord symbolsa modern “c/e” names a c chord with e in the bass. the historical figure 6 over e describes the intervals needed at that particular moment; the identity of the root is an analytical inference. the example moves through c, c/e and d minor/f before its dominant seventh and tonic. its upper voices are one possible realisation. the flexible notation constrains the harmony while leaving a trained player responsible for the texture and the local voice-leading.

title: Why can the same notes sound differently tuned?
sub: Temperament: where to put the discrepancy
k: why can the same notes sound differently tuned? temperament: where to put the discrepancy how it works tuning a pure fifth has a frequency ratio of 3:2. stack twelve such fifths and reduce by seven octaves: the result is 531441:524288, about 23.46 cents above unison. this difference is the pythagorean comma. on a keyboard with twelve notes per octave, closing the chain of fifths requires adjustment. pythagorean tuning also produces a major third of 81:64, appreciably wider than the pure 5:4 third. two commasthe syntonic comma, 81:80, is the difference between the pythagorean and pure major thirds. it is about 21.51 cents, compared with the pythagorean comma’s 23.46. a cent is one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone. quarter-comma meantone narrows the regular fifths by a quarter of the syntonic comma, about 5.38 cents. four such fifths then produce a pure major third after octave reduction. the price is that a conventional twelve-note layout cannot offer every enharmonic spelling: g♯ and a♭ would ideally require different keys. the closing interval becomes a conspicuous “wolf”. some historical keyboards supplied split accidentals to make more spellings available. meantone is a family of tunings; quarter-comma is one especially important member. unequal well temperaments distribute the adjustments so that all major and minor keys become usable, but their thirds and fifths retain different sizes. twelve-tone equal temperament instead gives every semitone the ratio 21/12. its fifth is 700 cents, slightly narrow; its major third is 400 cents, about 13.69 cents wider than 5:4. bach’s well-tempered clavier demonstrates access to all twenty-four keys while leaving the temperament unspecified. reconstructions of bach’s preferred tuning remain disputed. what beatsat a 220 hz base, compare the lower note’s third partial with the fifth’s second partial, or its fifth partial with the third’s fourth partial. their frequency difference gives the beat rate. these near-coincident pairs are upper partials. the laboratory makes that comparison with harmonic-rich tones. the equal-tempered fifth produces approximately 0.745 beats per second between 660 and 659.255 hz. the equal-tempered third produces 8.73 between 1100 and 1108.731 hz; the pythagorean third produces 13.75 between 1100 and 1113.75 hz. a pure interval removes the beating in the corresponding pair of partials; other interactions in a complex sound may remain. the printed example uses ordinary equal-tempered playback; the laboratory’s buttons change the frequency ratios. tuning laboratorypure fifth, 3:2equal-tempered fifthpure major third, 5:4equal-tempered thirdpythagorean thirdpress a button to hear two tones together, above a 220 hz base.

title: Why does one chord seem to need another?
sub: Harmony: a chord’s job depends on where it goes
k: why does one chord seem to need another? harmony: a chord’s job depends on where it goes how it works tonal direction in c major, c–e–g is the tonic triad, i; g–b–d is the dominant, v; f–a–c is the subdominant, iv. those labels locate roots in a scale. harmonic function describes their behaviour over time: tonic establishes or prolongs a centre, dominant directs attention towards it, and a predominant prepares the dominant. iv often serves as a predominant, but so does ii, d minor. a chord’s position in a phrase matters as much as the notes it contains. the dominant seventhg–b–d–f contains the tritone b–f. in a straightforward resolution to c major, b rises to c and f falls to e. the dissonance gives two independent voices specific destinations. a cadence closes a phrase. v–i can make an authentic cadence; its strongest textbook form has both roots in the bass and the tonic in the top voice of the final chord. a half cadence ends on v. a deceptive cadence redirects v, often to vi, deflecting the expected tonic. iv–i is called plagal. rhythm, melodic position and the preceding phrase determine whether these progressions close a phrase or occur in its middle. the circle of fifths orders keys by successive fifths: c, g, d, a, e, b, f♯ and their enharmonic continuations. adjacent major keys share six of their seven scale notes. this makes neighbouring keys convenient destinations for modulation. the same root relation can organise a sequence of chords in the opposite direction: e–a–d–g–c. in a diatonic sequence some chords are minor or diminished, and the bass can trace the circle of fifths within one key. tonicisation or modulationan applied dominant briefly treats another chord as a tonic. a modulation gives the new centre enough support — often a cadence and a sustained passage — to function as a key in its own right. to move from c major to g major, a minor can act as a pivot: vi in c becomes ii in g. d7 then introduces f♯, the new leading note, and resolves to g. the second example compresses that route into four bars; a full composition might delay its arrival with a sequence or extend the new tonic through several phrases. rameau’s traite de l’harmonie of 1722 helped establish analysis by chord roots and inversions. the later vocabulary of tonic, predominant and dominant describes relationships that continuo players also managed through bass motion and voice-leading.

title: Why does a returning tune feel different?
sub: Sonata form: the return changes the tonal route
k: why does a returning tune feel different? sonata form: the return changes the tonal route how it works large-scale tonality sonata form makes a large movement out of a tonal departure and a revised return. the exposition establishes the home key, then moves into a second key area and confirms it with cadential weight. in a major-key movement the second area is commonly the dominant; in a minor-key movement it is often the relative major. themes make these regions recognisable. a movement can reuse one theme in both areas and still make the tonal opposition unmistakable. exposition is a shared worda fugue’s exposition presents the voices in successive entries. a sonata exposition establishes a sequence of thematic functions and tonal areas. the development normally unsettles the exposition’s relatively stable regions. a short motive may be detached from its theme, passed between instruments, sequenced through several keys or combined with another fragment. some developments introduce new material. a retransition prepares the return, often by prolonging the home dominant. an almost motionless dominant pedal can make the coming tonic more urgent than a rapid succession of chords. the recapitulation returns the principal material but alters the tonal route. music previously directed towards a contrasting key must now be brought into the tonic region. that requires a rewritten transition, a transposed second group, or a less literal rearrangement. a coda can continue to develop the material after the main return. exposition repeats matter too: hearing the original route twice establishes expectations that the changed return can subsequently contradict. beethoven’s fifthin the first movement of symphony no. 5, op. 67, the exposition moves from c minor to e♭ major. the second group returns in c major during the recapitulation; the movement ultimately closes in c minor. beethoven’s fifth resolves a tonal difference while preserving the second group’s major quality: the move from e♭ major to c major changes its tonal centre. the first movement’s short-note motto also continues under contrasting material, binding the key areas together rhythmically. in the “waldstein” sonata, op. 53, beethoven stretches the convention further: c major’s exposition reaches e major in place of the usual g. its second group initially returns in a major before reaching the tonic. these are specific alternatives to a norm.

title: How do unexpected notes change a familiar harmony?
sub: Chromaticism: the spelling records the pressure
k: how do unexpected notes change a familiar harmony? chromaticism: the spelling records the pressure how it works altered scale degrees a chromatic note lies outside the prevailing diatonic collection. it may decorate a line without changing the harmony, alter a chord’s function, or prepare another key. these are different events: a passing c♯ between c and d need not announce d major. in nineteenth-century music, chromatic notes often make otherwise familiar functions more insistent. the decisive evidence is their resolution. two chords with the same piano keys can have different harmonic purposes if their notes are spelled and directed differently. neapolitanin c minor, the major triad on the lowered second degree is d♭–f–a♭. it commonly appears with f in the bass, hence “neapolitan sixth”, and usually prepares the dominant rather than establishing d♭ as a new tonic. an augmented-sixth chord puts the lowered sixth and raised fourth degrees around the dominant. in c, a♭ below f♯ expands outward to g–g. add c to obtain the italian form; add c and d for the french; add c and e♭ for the german. the national names are later classifications. the german form commonly moves through a cadential six-four before the dominant, avoiding the parallel fifths that a direct resolution can produce. enharmonic modulation changes a chord’s spelling and destination while preserving its sounding pitches in equal temperament. a♭–c–e♭–f♯, a german augmented sixth in c, can be respelled a♭–c–e♭–g♭, the dominant seventh of d♭. its outer notes take on new functions. fully diminished sevenths offer another resource: b–d–f–a♭ can point towards c; respelling a♭ as g♯ lets the same keyboard collection act as g♯–b–d–f, directed towards a. the musical context establishes the new interpretation. equal-tempered equivalencef♯ and g♭ share a key on a modern piano. they need not have identical frequencies in every historical tuning, or identical melodic inflections in a string quartet. chopin frequently embeds these resources within carefully directed inner voices: chromatic lines continue through the chord changes. his prelude in e minor, op. 28 no. 4, is a compact lesson in descending chromatic accompaniment beneath a restricted melody. liszt uses enharmonic reinterpretation to connect more distant regions within extended forms, including the sonata in b minor, s. 178. the invented examples isolate the harmonic mechanisms. follow each altered note to its destination.

title: Why does this chord leave us waiting?
sub: The Tristan chord: four notes, several readings
k: why does this chord leave us waiting? the tristan chord: four notes, several readings how it works a disputed sonority near the beginning of wagner’s tristan und isolde, the notes f–b–d♯–g♯ sound together. their spelling matters. above f, b is an augmented fourth, d♯ an augmented sixth, and g♯ an augmented ninth when placed in the upper register. the ensuing phrase reaches a dominant seventh on e, e–g♯–b–d. within the implied a minor, one unstable sonority has moved to another. the opening repeatedly develops this condition of arrival without final settlement. a familiar collection transformedrespell the chord f–a♭–c♭–e♭ and it becomes a half-diminished seventh. the novelty lies in the phrase’s voice-leading, rhythm, orchestration and withheld continuation. one functional reading hears g♯ as an appoggiatura, a leaning note that moves to a. the resulting f–a–b–d♯ has the pitch content of a french augmented sixth in a minor. it belongs to the predominant region and prepares e. this reading explains the chord through a familiar tonal function; its account must also follow the actual chromatic motion. other readings emphasise a decorated subdominant or interpret the initial notes as dissonant approaches to the dominant itself. a linear reading follows the individual voices before assigning a root to every vertical slice. the upper line’s g♯–a–a♯–b forms a melody through the changing chords. which notes count as structural and which as appoggiaturas depends on the span being analysed. a pitch-class description identifies the collection while leaving tonal function and the phrase’s direction open. these approaches answer different questions. the example’s scopethe two sustained chords in the opening example show the exact pitch collections f–b–d♯–g♯ and e–g♯–b–d. their durations and connecting voice-leading are schematic. the opera was first performed in munich in 1865. its influence on later harmony comes from the extension of these procedures across entire scenes. a dominant can remain intelligible while its expected tonic is postponed, redirected or concealed by another line. debussy later quotes the opening in “golliwogg’s cakewalk” from children’s corner: a recognisable dramatic manner becomes material for interruption and parody. tonal expectation makes the original chord’s deferred resolution audible.

title: How can a tune remember a character?
sub: Leitmotif: recognition with a changed meaning
k: how can a tune remember a character? leitmotif: recognition with a changed meaning how it works musical memory a leitmotif is a recurring musical idea associated with a dramatic person, object, action or concept. the music can recall that association independently of spoken words. in wagner’s ring, the orchestra can recall a promise that a character conceals, anticipate an object before it becomes visible, or combine motives whose dramatic meanings are in conflict. a short interval pattern may carry the identity; rhythm, register and instrumentation help the listener recognise it under changing harmonies. names as listening aidsmany familiar motive labels were circulated by commentators, notably hans von wolzogen. a label identifies a first association, leaving later uses open. the sword nothung gives a concrete example of musical memory extending beyond a single scene. its associations pass through das rheingold, die walkure and siegfried, even though the sword’s dramatic condition changes from promise to possession, fragments and reforging. the orchestra can connect those states before a spectator consciously identifies the notes. a change of harmony or a collision with another motive can enrich the association. the technique has several predecessors. berlioz’s symphonie fantastique (1830) carries an idee fixe, associated with the beloved, through five movements; in the finale its appearance on e♭ clarinet changes both register and character. liszt’s thematic transformation similarly preserves a theme’s identity while changing its tempo, metre or harmonic setting. recurrence, transformation and dramatic association overlap while remaining distinct procedures. three kinds of changetransposition moves a pattern to another pitch level. augmentation lengthens its durations proportionally. reharmonisation changes the supporting chords without necessarily changing the melody. each can preserve different identifying features. the example uses an invented c–e–g cell. lowering e changes its mode while preserving the contour; halving the durations changes its pace; doubling them makes the same proportions extend across a barline. a real leitmotif may survive less literal transformations, particularly when an orchestral colour or dramatic context supplies the missing clue. to follow one through an opera, compare its bass and inner voices as well as its melody. a familiar tune above a new bass can disclose a changed allegiance even when its surface rhythm remains intact.

title: Can the same notes make different scales?
sub: Modes: change the centre, change the intervals
k: can the same notes make different scales? modes: change the centre, change the intervals how it works diatonic alternatives the white notes of the piano can support several centres. give d that role and the collection forms d dorian: d–e–f–g–a–b–c. its minor third coexists with a major sixth, b, rather than the b♭ of natural minor. e phrygian places a semitone immediately above its centre, e–f. f lydian has a raised fourth, b, compared with f major. g mixolydian has a lowered seventh, f, compared with g major. a sustained bass, phrase endings and recurring melodic shapes establish which note acts as centre. medieval modes are more than scaleshistorical church-mode classification also concerns final, range and reciting tone, with authentic and plagal forms. modern modal composition often borrows interval patterns without reproducing that complete system. transposition carries the interval pattern to a new pitch level. c lydian therefore needs f♯; d mixolydian needs f♯ and c♮. a dorian tune may remain recognisably modal even when its harmony occasionally uses a leading note at a cadence. modes can govern a phrase, a pedal passage or a thematic strand while the surrounding music works through ordinary major–minor tonality. sibelius’s sixth symphony, op. 104 (1923), draws much of its opening string writing from a dorian-inflected d centre. the natural sixth alters the minor colour without requiring a chromatic detour. vaughan williams’s fantasia on a theme by thomas tallis (1910) takes its principal melody from tallis’s third tune for archbishop parker’s psalter, published in 1567; its phrygian inheritance contributes to the expanded string-orchestra setting’s harmonic vocabulary. listen to the distinctive degreedorian: natural sixth in a minor collection. phrygian: lowered second. lydian: raised fourth in a major collection. mixolydian: lowered seventh. these comparisons assume the same tonic. debussy combines modal and symmetrical collections. in l’isle joyeuse (1904), a lydian belongs to a network that also includes a major, whole-tone material and the acoustic collection a–b–c♯–d♯–e–f♯–g. the last collection’s natural g distinguishes it from ordinary lydian. dmitri tymoczko’s analysis of debussy’s scale networks traces these small changes between collections. the two scale examples isolate the distinctive degrees for comparison.

title: What happens when every scale step is equal?
k: what happens when every scale step is equal? whole-tone harmony: no privileged semitone how it works six equal steps a whole-tone scale divides the octave into six equal whole tones: c–d–e–f♯–g♯–a♯–c. it contains no semitone and no perfect fifth. every note has the same interval environment, placing c, d and f♯ on equal terms within the collection. a bass pedal, accent or melodic recurrence can still establish a centre. only two collectionstranspose a whole-tone collection up a semitone and obtain the other one. transpose it up a whole tone and recover the original pitch classes in a different order. messiaen classified it as his first mode of limited transposition. taking alternate notes produces an augmented triad: c–e–g♯. its three major thirds divide the octave equally, making its inversions sound less differentiated than those of a major triad. d–f♯–a♯ supplies the other augmented triad within the same whole-tone collection. chords can move in parallel while staying inside the scale. the bass and the duration of each sonority can supply direction independently of dominant–tonic functions. debussy’s piano prelude voiles, published in book i in 1910, uses whole-tone material for most of its span, with a contrasting pentatonic passage. the contrast matters because a five-note collection restores unequal interval sizes, including minor thirds, which the whole-tone field excludes. its title can mean either “sails” or “veils”. a sustained b♭ gives the symmetrical field a reference point outside conventional b♭ major or minor. a russian precedentglinka used whole-tone material in ruslan and lyudmila (1842), notably in the supernatural associations around chernomor. russian composers developed that vocabulary before debussy’s piano preludes. whole-tone passages can also arise locally inside tonal music: an altered dominant may share several of their notes. the analyst must distinguish a complete governing collection from a brief chord that happens to fit one. an ornamental chromatic note can occur within a whole-tone passage while its stable degrees remain intact. in the example, the two augmented triads partition all six notes. their relationship is one of register and pitch level, independent of a leading note or a perfect-fifth root relation.

title: What can a scale of eight notes do?
sub: Octatonic harmony: alternating whole tones and semitones
k: what can a scale of eight notes do? octatonic harmony: alternating whole tones and semitones how it works eight-note symmetry an octatonic collection alternates semitones and whole tones. beginning with a semitone on c gives c–d♭–e♭–e–f♯–g–a–b♭. the octave contains eight pitch classes, compared with the seven of a diatonic scale or six of a whole-tone scale. starting with a whole tone on c selects a different member of the octatonic family. once the starting collection is chosen, its rotations preserve the alternation. three distinct collectionstransposition by a minor third reproduces an octatonic collection. transpositions by zero, one and two semitones therefore exhaust its distinct pitch-class collections. messiaen’s mode 2 names this symmetry as limited transposition. the collection contains two interlocking diminished-seventh chords. in the example they are f♯–a–c–e♭ and c♯–e–g–b♭, with c♯ enharmonically equivalent to the scale’s d♭. it also contains several ordinary major and minor triads. a composer can consequently establish a recognisable chord locally while placing it in a larger, symmetrical field. a major triad’s bass, repetition and relation to the other chords determine how much tonal authority it acquires. rimsky-korsakov explored the collection in the orchestral tableau sadko, op. 5 (1867), well before the later opera of that name. its use became associated with supernatural episodes in his operas, often contrasted with more diatonic music for human characters. stravinsky, who studied with him, adapted octatonic resources to more abrupt juxtapositions and repeating blocks. octatonic relationships are one resource within the varied pitch language of petrushka and the rite of spring. a specific superpositionthe famous c-major/f♯-major “petrushka chord” places two triads together. the ballet also draws on other collections, tonal references and changes of pitch organisation. messiaen made the three transpositions of mode 2 explicit in his technique de mon langage musical (1944). his practice combines the eight-note scale with particular chord voicings, colours and rhythmic procedures. in an octatonic passage, listen for minor-third-related transpositions and for chords that change while remaining within the same collection. unlike the whole-tone scale, this one supplies semitones in abundance; their symmetrical placement gives several notes a potential claim to centrality.

title: What holds music together without a home key?
sub: Atonality: organised intervals without a home key
k: what holds music together without a home key? atonality: organised intervals without a home key how it works without a tonic atonal music organises pitch outside the governing tonic hierarchy of major–minor harmony. it can use repetition, melody and consonant intervals. the question is whether one pitch or triad controls the others as a tonal centre over the relevant span. a dense chromatic passage in wagner can preserve that control; a spare line in webern can dispense with it. before twelve-tone compositionschoenberg’s three piano pieces, op. 11 (1909), precede his twelve-tone method. atonality and serialism describe distinct historical and technical developments. without dominant-to-tonic syntax, other relationships become more exposed. a three-note cell can recur at a new pitch level, turn upside down, expand into a chord or pass between instruments. its intervals may remain recognisable even when its register and rhythm change. a pitch-class analysis treats octave-equivalent notes as members of the same class, making some of these relations easier to describe. such a reduction leaves out register, dynamics and articulation, all of which may be essential to the phrase as heard. in the example, c–c♯–f contains an ascending semitone followed by a major third. g–g♯–c transposes that pattern up a fifth. c–b–g reverses the interval directions, producing an inversion, and d–c♯–a transposes that inversion. these controlled relationships connect the cells independently of a v–i cadence, offering one way of relating events outside a key. consonance can remain locala major third or perfect fifth inside an atonal piece is still audible as an interval. what disappears is the assumption that it must belong to a tonic, dominant or another chord within a single key. schoenberg’s erwartung, op. 17 (1909), uses the continuity of a dramatic monologue; webern’s short instrumental works concentrate on register, silence and articulation; berg retains tonal references and familiar forms within a more mixed language. each score’s organisation emerges through its intervals, rhythms and returns. kandinsky’s response to schoenberg in 1911 supplies a documented connection with painting.

title: Can an ordered set of notes shape music?
sub: Twelve-tone writing: a row orders pitch classes
k: can an ordered set of notes shape music? twelve-tone writing: a row orders pitch classes how it works ordered pitch classes a twelve-tone row orders the twelve chromatic pitch classes, each appearing once. it leaves rhythm, register, dynamics and instrumentation open. a composer can distribute its notes between melody and accompaniment, combine successive notes into chords, repeat an immediately sounding note, or articulate groups from the row as motives. the classroom injunction “never repeat a note until all twelve have sounded” oversimplifies this freedom. schoenberg’s op. 25the basic row is e–f–g–d♭–g♭–e♭–a♭–d–b–c–a–b♭. the suite for piano was composed in 1921–23. its last four notes, read backwards, give b♭–a–c–b: b–a–c–h in german note names. the prime form presents the chosen order. inversion reverses each directed pitch-class interval: if the prime moves up one semitone, the inversion moves down one. retrograde reverses the order of the notes; retrograde inversion reverses the inverted order. each of these four forms can be transposed to twelve pitch levels, giving forty-eight standard forms before any coincidences caused by a row’s own symmetry. their relationships preserve specific interval successions or reverse their direction and order. the examples keep the inversion’s initial e fixed. e–f becomes e–e♭, and the following upward whole tone f–g becomes the downward whole tone e♭–d♭. all notes are placed within one illustrative octave to expose pitch classes. the schematic barlines divide each row into three groups of four. labelling systems differ about whether the chosen prime is called p0 or, with c numbered zero, p4. stating the initial pitch avoids that ambiguity here. a restricted selectionthe arnold schonberg center’s account notes that op. 25 uses only eight of the forty-eight forms: the four basic operations and their tritone transpositions. its dances — gavotte, musette, menuett and gigue — retain historical formal references while the pitch organisation changes. the row can function as a shared interval resource across different movements. webern would exploit rows with strong internal symmetries; berg chose rows that could expose tonal allusions. later serial composers extended ordering procedures to durations or dynamics. within the twelve-tone method, rhythm and phrase shape remain compositional decisions.

title: Why can a steady beat feel off balance?
sub: Rhythm: pulse and accent can diverge
k: why can a steady beat feel off balance? rhythm: pulse and accent can diverge how it works grouping time metre groups recurring pulses into a hierarchy of stronger and weaker positions. rhythm is the actual pattern of attacks, durations and silences placed against that grouping. a melody can contradict the metre while the accompaniment maintains it. in a hemiola, six equal units are regrouped from two groups of three into three groups of two, or the reverse. across two bars of 3/4, three minims can therefore displace the expected two sets of three crotchets without changing the underlying duration. hemiola is not a tempo changethe span stays the same. what changes is the location of the grouping accents. renaissance cadences, baroque dances and brahms’s phrase extensions use the device in different textures. additive rhythm constructs a longer group from unequal smaller units. a 7/8 bar can divide 2+2+3. balkan aksak patterns combine short and long groups, commonly in a 2:3 relation. bartok’s six dances in bulgarian rhythm at the end of mikrokosmos, nos. 148–153, make such groupings explicit; no. 148 uses 4+2+3. the larger pulses depend on the grouping as well as the notated denominator. stravinsky uses changing bar lengths in the “sacrificial dance” of the rite of spring, making a steady small unit support unevenly returning accents. elsewhere in the ballet, displaced accents operate within an unchanged metre. messiaen’s added values modify an existing duration with a short note, a rest or a dot. extending a two-quaver unit to three quavers shifts everything that follows by one quaver; a new time signature may record the effect, but the generative idea is the addition. non-retrogradable rhythma duration sequence such as 2–3–2 reads identically forwards and backwards. messiaen uses this separate property alongside added values. asymmetry and rhythmic palindromes are independent properties. polyrhythm sounds different regular divisions of the same span simultaneously. in three against two, one part makes three equally spaced attacks while another makes two. dividing the span into six subunits locates the first part at 0, 2 and 4, the second at 0 and 3. both return together at 6. this differs from alternating a bar in three with a bar in two, and from polymetre, where parts maintain different metrical groupings. the examples keep the pitches simple to focus the comparison on the attacks.

title: How does changing instruments change a tune?
sub: Orchestration: register, balance and the attack of a note
k: how does changing instruments change a tune? orchestration: register, balance and the attack of a note how it works instrumental construction orchestration assigns musical material to instruments and changes its effect. a flute projects differently in its low and high registers; a horn can merge with woodwind or become a distinct brass voice. a clarinet note with a gentle attack can enter beneath a string tone and temporarily conceal its source. register, articulation and dynamic determine whether a line separates from its surroundings or combines with another instrument into a composite sound. two working booksberlioz’s grand traite d’instrumentation et d’orchestration modernes appeared in 1843–44. rimsky-korsakov’s posthumous principles of orchestration, edited by maximilian steinberg, organises practical questions of balance, doubling and the distribution of parts. berlioz describes instrumental mechanisms and ranges alongside their dramatic uses, illustrating his claims with passages from actual scores. rimsky-korsakov separates problems such as a melody in octaves, sustained harmony and accompaniment, testing how orchestral families combine. applying either book requires knowledge of the particular player or instrument. a written note has different consequences on a stopped horn, a muted trumpet and an open string, even when the sounding frequency agrees. ravel’s bolero (1928) holds its principal rhythmic ostinato and melodic material relatively constant while changing instrumental presentation and accumulating weight. the first melody arrives on solo flute; later statements exploit instruments including saxophones and trombone. a particularly instructive combination uses horn, celesta and piccolos at different pitch levels to suggest the components of a composite timbre. the harmony’s long stability makes those changes unusually exposed. the work also contains a late tonal disruption. doubling has a costadding instruments can thicken a line without making its articulation clearer. a low, widely spaced chord may project better than the same notes crowded together in the bass, where their partials overlap densely. extended techniques change the method of sound production: sul ponticello places the bow near the bridge, col legno uses its wood, and wind multiphonics use specialised fingerings and embouchures to produce several components together. their notation must specify a reproducible action. the example assigns the same notes to flute and oboe so that timbre is the only intended variable. its general midi playback demonstrates instrumental assignment in isolation from a live player’s breath, attack, dynamics and room.

title: How can repetition make something new?
sub: Minimalism: repetition makes the change measurable
k: how can repetition make something new? minimalism: repetition makes the change measurable how it works audible processes terry riley’s in c (1964) provides fifty-three short patterns in a fixed order. each player chooses how often to repeat a pattern before advancing, listening to the ensemble throughout. a repeated high c commonly supplies the quaver pulse. the resulting overlaps vary between performances, but the order of the material and the shared pulse constrain the freedom. “repeat” asks the performer to maintain a relationship. different processesriley’s performers occupy different points in a shared sequence. reich’s phasing shifts the alignment of the same repeating pattern. glass’s additive process changes a pattern’s length. in reich’s piano phase (1967), two performers initially align a repeating figure. one gradually moves ahead until the patterns settle one subdivision apart; the process proceeds through further alignments. new composite patterns emerge from the combination of the two parts. the opening example presents two fixed alignments, illustrating the destination of a phase shift through an abrupt displacement. philip glass’s two pages explores the extension and contraction of a line through additive process. a schematic c–d–e might become c–d–e–g, then c–d–e–g–a before contracting again. the common pulse remains, but the cycle takes longer to recur. glass’s work with ravi shankar and alla rakha helped direct his attention towards grouping small rhythmic units into larger spans. his published recording notes describe two pages as an early study of precisely this expansion and contraction. tintinnabuli is a separate syntaxpart combines a melodic voice with a voice drawn from a fixed triad. rules choose the triadic note’s position relative to the melody, determining pitch relationships independently of loops or phase processes. part’s fur alina (1976) is an early statement of tintinnabuli. a stepwise melody and a triadic partner generate intervals that can sound exposed; silence and the piano’s decay are part of their articulation. the second example uses an explicitly invented rule: accompany each melody note with the nearest strictly lower member of a–c–e. calling riley, reich, glass and part “minimalist” identifies a broad history of reduced materials and repetition. their pieces differ in who controls the process, which elements change, and how a phrase comes to an end.

title: Can one sound supply a whole harmony?
sub: Spectralism: a timbre becomes harmonic material
k: can one sound supply a whole harmony? spectralism: a timbre becomes harmonic material how it works inside the sound a harmonic spectrum contains components at whole-number multiples of a fundamental frequency: f, 2f, 3f, 4f and so on. its spacing is uneven when heard as musical intervals: the first two components form an octave, the next pair a fifth, and higher neighbours become progressively closer. their relative strengths and their behaviour during the attack and decay help determine timbre. spectral composition uses such frequency relationships and changes over time as material for harmony, orchestration and form. partials and harmonicsa partial is a component of a complex sound. a harmonic partial is an integer multiple of the fundamental. bells and other inharmonic sounds supply spectral music with different frequency relations. gerard grisey’s partiels (1975), for eighteen musicians, opens around a low e and spreads a harmonic field across instrumental registers. the ensemble can be heard as separate notes or as a composite sound; changing their entrances, intensity and tuning changes that perception. francois-xavier feron’s research in the sketches distinguishes the early works’ constructed spectra from the later use of measured sonographic data. a source correctionin his 2022 ircam presentation, feron states that no trombone sound served as the model for periodes or partiels; direct spectral analyses informed sections of later works including modulations and transitoires. tristan murail’s gondwana (1980) brings inharmonic, bell-like fields into relation with more harmonic spectra. electronic synthesis supplies compositional models even when the performing medium is an orchestra: calculated frequency relationships can become instrumental pitches, and changes of spectral density can govern a transition. real instruments contribute spectra of their own, making the ensemble sound an interpretation of the model. the seventh harmonic illustrates why conventional notation needs qualification. above an e fundamental it lies near d, about 31.17 cents below the equal-tempered pitch; the fifth harmonic lies about 13.69 cents below an equal-tempered g♯. quarter-tone or finer notation can approximate these relations, but a normal piano cannot tune them independently. the invented example plays equal-tempered landmarks. grisey’s later l’icone paradoxale adds another form of modelling: piero della francesca’s spatial proportions and writings on perspective enter the construction of musical time and vocal material.

title: Why does a shorter string sound higher?
k: why does a shorter string sound higher? a string divided before bach c. 530 bc pythagoras settled at croton in southern italy around 530 bc. he left no writings, and the musical discoveries attached to his name belong to a tradition assembled by later authors. what survives is a proposition that could be tested: the octave, fifth and fourth correspond to small whole-number ratios. music already had long histories in mesopotamia, egypt and greece. the ratios made its intervals available to mathematical demonstration. the blacksmith storylater writers describe pythagoras discovering consonance from hammers of different weights. the experiment does not work as told: hammer weight alone does not determine pitch, and string frequency varies with the square root of tension, not directly with the suspended weight. a monochord is one string stretched over a resonating box, with a movable bridge that changes its vibrating length. keep the string’s tension and mass per unit length constant and halve that length: the frequency doubles, producing an octave. stop the string at two-thirds of its original length and the frequency becomes three-halves, a perfect fifth above the original note. three-quarters of the length gives four-thirds of the frequency, a perfect fourth. the frequency ratios are therefore 2:1, 3:2 and 4:3; the corresponding length ratios run in the opposite direction. a fifth divided by a fourth gives 9:8, the pythagorean whole tone. a real stretched string also vibrates in several patterns at once. its whole length produces the fundamental; two equal sections produce the second partial, three sections the third, and so on. for an ideal flexible string these frequencies form the harmonic series: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 times the fundamental. over c, the first six partials are c, c, g, c, e and g in successively higher registers. the third partial is a fifth above the second, the fourth a fourth above the third. the fifth introduces the pure major third, 5:4, above the fourth. harmonic series sixteen partialsthe diagram gives integer multiples of c’s frequency. the seventh partial lies about 31 cents below the nearest equal-tempered b♭; the eleventh lies about 49 cents below f♯. a cent is one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone. the harmonic series supplies a modern acoustical explanation. pythagorean tuning builds notes from successive pure fifths; its major third is 81:64, wider than the series’ 5:4. a flute, a violin and a voice emphasise their partials differently, which helps distinguish their timbres even on the same pitch. bells and other vibrating bodies can have strongly inharmonic partials, whose frequencies depart from whole-number multiples of one fundamental. boethius’s de institutione musica, written around the beginning of the sixth century ad, carried greek mathematical theory into latin education. music joined arithmetic, geometry and astronomy in the quadrivium: number studied in relation to sounding intervals. ancient theorists organised scales through tetrachords — four notes spanning a fourth — and used terms such as harmonia and tonos in several distinct senses. the greek names dorian, phrygian and lydian were later reassigned to church modes. ancient greek dorian and medieval dorian name different octave arrangements. a modern white-note scale from d to d is a useful first model of church dorian. the names survived through changes of theory, repertory and musical practice.

title: How can one melody carry a whole service?
k: how can one melody carry a whole service? one line, many functions before bach c. 750–1200 gregorian chant is a repertory of latin liturgical melodies bearing the name of pope gregory the great. gregory died in 604; the repertory’s decisive formation and dissemination belong to the eighth- and ninth-century encounter between roman worship and the frankish church under the carolingians. its exact relationship to the separately transmitted old roman chant remains a subject of scholarship. the papal name gave authority to a body of music transmitted first through singers, then through books. chant is monophonic: one melodic line, whether sung by a soloist or a group. it serves two large structures, the mass and the divine office, the daily cycle of services organised around psalms, readings and prayers. the mass ordinary includes recurring texts such as the kyrie, gloria and sanctus; the proper supplies texts that change with the day or feast. a syllabic chant gives mostly one note to each syllable. a melismatic chant stretches a syllable over many notes, sometimes turning one vowel into a substantial musical span. four finals, eight modesmodes 1–2 end normally on d, 3–4 on e, 5–6 on f and 7–8 on g. the odd-numbered modes are authentic; their even-numbered partners are plagal. these eight categories describe melodic behaviour. the eight-mode system classified chants by their final, range and characteristic melodic relationships. an authentic melody generally occupies the octave above its final, with some extension below; a plagal melody places the same final more centrally in its range. the customary names are dorian and hypodorian, phrygian and hypophrygian, lydian and hypolydian, mixolydian and hypomixolydian. actual melodies often exceed the textbook compass. b♭ can appear where a white-note diagram would suggest b♮, and some older chants fit their assigned category imperfectly. a psalm tone is a reusable formula. an opening intonation leads to a reciting pitch on which many syllables can be sung; a cadence marks the middle of the verse, and another closes it. the amount of recitation expands or contracts with the words. an antiphon, a short chant sung around the psalm, determines the appropriate tone and ending. modal classification thus solved a practical problem: how to connect hundreds of different antiphons with a manageable stock of psalm formulas. reading a gesturestaffless neumes record ascent, descent, grouping and details of delivery without consistently fixing interval size. the st gall cantatorium, copied in the early tenth century, preserves exceptionally detailed signs for solo chants. the earliest neumes sit above the text like marks of vocal movement. they usually assume that the singer already knows the melody. later heighted notation makes relative pitch more visible, and the staff fixes it more precisely. rhythmic interpretation remains less secure. the latin accent, the grouping of notes and the liturgical sentence all shape delivery. the dies irae is a later medieval sequence. its opening stanza describes the day of judgement and invokes david and the sibyl as witnesses. the tune begins f–e–f–d–e–c–d–d, returning repeatedly to d without a leading-note c♯. berlioz quotes it in the symphonie fantastique; rachmaninoff repeatedly uses its opening contour. hildegard of bingen’s twelfth-century songs show a different extension of monophony: unusually wide ranges and long melismas, composed for a women’s religious community.

title: What happens when chant gains another voice?
sub: A second voice above the chant
k: what happens when chant gains another voice? a second voice above the chant before bach c. 900–1200 the anonymous ninth-century treatise musica enchiriadis describes ways of singing a second part with a chant. some passages proceed in parallel fourths or fifths, sometimes doubled at the octave; others hold one voice still while the other moves, allowing the parts to meet in unison. the treatise gives a written account of these polyphonic practices. organum encompasses several changing techniques. in the simplest parallel model, every note of a melody acquires a companion at a constant interval. in more independent writing, the voices can move in contrary directions, embellish their approach to a consonance or place several notes against one. eleventh- and twelfth-century sources show a growing distance between the borrowed chant and the newly composed part. the chant supplies an inherited sequence; the added voice decides how much time each part of that sequence will occupy. the tenor holdstenor comes from latin tenere, to hold. here it names the part that holds the pre-existing chant. a single tenor note can support a long phrase in the upper voice. in late-twelfth-century paris, the repertory associated with notre-dame developed this contrast on a much larger scale. leonin is linked with the magnus liber organi, the ‘great book of organum’, a collection for important services. in sustained-note passages, one chant note lies underneath a freely unfolding upper line. in discant passages, both voices move in coordinated measured rhythm. a setting can pass between these textures and plainchant, reserving polyphonic elaboration for particular liturgical portions. our principal account of leonin and perotin comes from a later thirteenth-century theorist conventionally called anonymous iv. he credits leonin with the great book and describes perotin’s revisions and compositions in three and four parts. the surviving manuscripts preserve a repertory copied and altered by successive musicians. the familiar connection between perotin’s four-part viderunt omnes and christmas 1198 rests on historical reconstruction. rhythmic modespatterns of long and short values organise the upper parts. the shape and grouping of ligatures — several notes joined as one written sign — help indicate the pattern. here ‘mode’ describes a rhythmic arrangement. viderunt omnes elaborates the christmas gradual whose text begins ‘all the ends of the earth have seen the salvation of our god’. three upper parts move above the chant-bearing tenor. at the opening, the first syllable is extended so far that the listener hears changing rhythmic combinations before hearing a complete word. repeated figures pass between voices; coordinated rests expose the separate strands; unisons, fifths and octaves articulate points of arrival. the governing contrast is between the very slow progress of the inherited melody and the faster activity above it. a discant section could be detached and replaced by another setting of the same tenor fragment: such a unit is called a clausula. adding words to an upper part helped generate the thirteenth-century motet, in which different voices could eventually sing different texts at once. the route from chant to polyphony was therefore also a route from one shared liturgical utterance to several simultaneous layers of language. counterpoint begins with the practical task of making those independent lines agree at chosen moments.

title: How did singers learn unfamiliar music?
sub: A melody that can be read
k: how did singers learn unfamiliar music? a melody that can be read before bach c. 1025 guido of arezzo, a benedictine monk active in the early eleventh century, addressed a costly part of a singer’s education: learning an enormous repertory by repetition. his micrologus, written around 1025–28, and his other teaching texts combine interval theory with practical methods for reading unfamiliar chant. earlier musicians had used pitch letters, reference lines and heighted neumes. guido made these resources into a teachable system. a staff gives pitch a repeatable location. a line labelled f or c fixes the surrounding succession of tones and semitones; the spaces count as positions just as the lines do. coloured reference lines could make f and c recognisable before the singer read a letter. four-line staves became standard in square chant notation after a period of varied layouts. the five-line staff familiar from a piano score was a later convention. a clef is a letterthe c and f clefs identify one staff position, from which the others can be inferred. a change of clef need not change the melody: it can keep a wide-ranging phrase on the same small staff. guido also described learning intervals through a familiar hymn to john the baptist, ut queant laxis. in the teaching melody, six successive phrases begin one degree higher: c, d, e, f, g, a. their opening syllables supply ut, re, mi, fa, sol, la: ut queant laxis / resonare fibris / mira gestorum / famuli tuorum / solve polluti / labii reatum. the singer recalls a known phrase to find an unknown note. the crucial small interval is always mi–fa, the semitone between the third and fourth steps. later medieval teaching developed this into overlapping six-note units, or hexachords. the natural hexachord begins on c; the hard hexachord on g includes b♮; the soft hexachord on f includes b♭. each has the same interval pattern: tone, tone, semitone, tone, tone. a melody extending beyond six notes requires a change of hexachord, called mutation. the pitch itself need not change when its syllable does: g can be sol in the natural hexachord and ut in the hard one. six syllablesthe seventh syllable si and the replacement do belong to solmisation histories later than guido’s method. in the medieval system, each syllable can move between pitches. the guidonian hand puts the gamut — the available succession of named pitches — onto the joints and fingertips of a left hand. a teacher can point to a location; a singer retrieves its pitch-name and possible syllables. surviving hand diagrams belong to the later transmission of guidonian pedagogy; attribution of the familiar diagram to guido himself remains uncertain. the painted hand is both a picture and a working memory aid: spatial position carries information that would otherwise have to be recited. notation expanded the written record while oral teaching continued. a staff can specify the interval between two notes while leaving pronunciation, vocal production and much rhythmic detail to the community that uses it. it also makes comparison possible: the same melody can be copied, corrected and discussed far from its original singers. when musicians begin coordinating independent lines in organum, that stable record of pitch becomes indispensable; exact duration will require another set of inventions.

title: Can a rhythm repeat while its notes change?
k: can a rhythm repeat while its notes change? time can be counted twice before bach c. 1320–1370 around 1320, french musicians acquired more precise ways of writing divisions of musical time. the label ars nova, ‘new art’, is associated with philippe de vitry and the theoretical writings transmitted under his name. thirteenth-century mensural notation, particularly that described by franco of cologne, had already made note shapes carry durational information. fourteenth-century practice extended the system’s treatment of smaller values, binary division and syncopation. mensuration specifies how one value divides into the next. a breve can contain three semibreves, called perfect tempus, or two, imperfect tempus; a semibreve can contain three minims, major prolation, or two, minor prolation. these two decisions are independent. a circle and a semicircle, with or without a dot, eventually provide a compact visual vocabulary for the combinations. our c-shaped common-time sign descends from the semicircle. duration in contextmedieval note values can change through context, imperfection, alteration and coloration. these rules determine the notes’ actual durations alongside the mensural sign. isorhythm separates a repeating rhythmic pattern from a repeating sequence of pitches. the rhythmic pattern is conventionally called the talea; the pitch sequence, the color. their lengths need not agree. if three durations cycle through a five-note melody, the two beginnings meet again only after fifteen note attacks. a composer can also restate a rhythmic structure at a changed proportional speed. the procedure is especially associated with the tenor of fourteenth-century motets, although other voices may participate in the design. the scheme becomes audible through its effects. a returning tenor rhythm regulates where upper voices can settle, where a cadence can arrive and where a new span begins. above it, syncopation can carry a note across an expected division, and hocket can split a line between voices by alternating notes and rests. vitry’s motets combine these resources with texts that can address political and ecclesiastical circumstances. the composed surface moves against a framework whose repetitions are often slower than an ordinary melodic phrase. a modern analytical namethe term ‘isorhythm’ was coined long after the medieval repertory to identify a compositional procedure. guillaume de machaut, a poet as well as a composer, brought together courtly song, motet and large-scale sacred music. his four-voice messe de nostre dame, usually dated to the 1360s, is the earliest surviving complete polyphonic mass ordinary attributed to one composer. it includes kyrie, gloria, credo, sanctus, agnus dei and ite, missa est. earlier polyphonic mass movements and assembled cycles survive. its precise original occasion remains unknown; the familiar claim that it was written for charles v’s coronation in 1364 is unsupported. the shorter texts — kyrie, sanctus, agnus dei and dismissal — permit chant-based isorhythmic construction. the long gloria and credo move much more often in syllabic, coordinated declamation. a contratenor works against the tenor, while the two upper parts can carry more active lines; the lowest sounding part can change as the voices move. machaut’s secular ballades, rondeaux and virelais organise another kind of recurrence through poetic refrains and fixed forms. his manuscript collections place music alongside narrative poems, making the control of musical time one part of a larger practice of authorship.

title: Why do different instruments sustain notes differently?
k: why do different instruments sustain notes differently? wood, gut, wind and wire before bach c. 1400–1700 the instruments of bach’s ensembles had separate histories. church organs, courtly lutes, domestic viol consorts and professional violin bands developed in different settings, with different ways of producing and sustaining a note. their mechanisms mattered to composition. an organ can hold a tone while the key remains down and wind is supplied; a lute or harpsichord note begins to decay as soon as its string has been plucked. a bowed instrument can change pressure and speed during a single note. the organ’s ancestry reaches back to the ancient mediterranean hydraulis, whose water mechanism regulated wind pressure. medieval european organs used bellows, and by the later middle ages builders were separating ranks of pipes into selectable stops. a stop gives access to a set of pipes with a particular construction and pitch level. at an 8-foot pitch a key sounds at its ordinary register, a 4-foot rank an octave higher, a 16-foot rank an octave lower. multiple manuals and pedal keyboards eventually let an organist distribute parts and colours between hands and feet. what eight feet meansthe foot designation refers to the nominal length of an open pipe at the bottom of a rank. stopped pipes can sound the same pitch at roughly half that length. mixture stops combine several higher ranks. the european lute derives from the arabic ʿud, transmitted through mediterranean contact. its rounded back, fretted neck and paired strings, called courses, support both accompaniment and independent polyphony. renaissance players could reduce a vocal piece to one instrument, deciding which voices to sustain, repeat or ornament when several lines competed for the same hand. tablature often records where the fingers go rather than giving every sounding pitch on a staff. longer-necked bass members of the lute family, especially the theorbo, later supplied low notes and chords to the continuo group. viols and violins form distinct, related bowed families. renaissance viols usually have frets and six strings tuned mainly in fourths with a central third; they are supported against or between the legs, including the smaller sizes. their consort repertory distributes polyphonic lines among treble, tenor and bass instruments. the violin family normally has four strings tuned in fifths and no frets. its curved bridge helps the bow select one string, while the fretless fingerboard lets the left hand adjust intonation freely. the cremonese traditionandrea amati’s surviving sixteenth-century instruments are central evidence for the early violin family. nicolo amati and antonio stradivari developed the cremonese tradition in the seventeenth century. a formal apprenticeship of stradivari to nicolo remains uncertain. andrea amati, his descendants and the other cremonese workshops established models that later makers repeatedly studied. stradivari’s career extended into bach’s lifetime; he died in 1737. many old instruments subsequently acquired altered necks, bass bars and other fittings, combining a seventeenth-century body with a later playing setup. early violin ensembles served dances, ceremonies and theatre as well as the developing sonata. sixteenth-century bass instruments varied in size and tuning; the cello’s orchestral prominence came later. a harpsichord key raises a jack whose plectrum plucks a string; a damper stops the string when the key is released. its rectangular relatives include the virginals, familiar from dutch paintings. unlike a piano, the harpsichord does not normally make a note louder simply because the player strikes the key harder. articulation, timing, added notes and changes of register produce its contrasts. it can therefore sustain the harmonic outline of a vocal piece through repeated or newly voiced chords even while each individual string is decaying.

title: How can several voices each tell a story?
k: how can several voices each tell a story? each voice has a sentence before bach c. 1430–1600 guillaume dufay worked across the church and court networks that connected northern france, the low countries and italy. his motet nuper rosarum flores was written for the consecration of florence cathedral in 1436. its large-scale proportional design retains an isorhythmic inheritance, while the sonorities of fifteenth-century music increasingly make room for thirds and sixths. the changing treatment of these familiar intervals altered how voices could combine between the open fifths and octaves of cadences. a cantus firmus — literally a ‘fixed song’ — can organise an entire mass by returning in successive movements. it may come from chant or from a secular melody such as l’homme arme, which dufay and many later composers used. a voice may present it slowly while other parts move faster; a composer may change its register, proportion or position in the texture. another technique, fauxbourdon, produces chains of sixth-chord sonorities through a partly prescribed relationship between voices. each part retains its own melodic progress within these sonorities. imitation is an entryone part states a melodic idea; another begins the same idea later, often at a different pitch. a point of imitation can run through the ensemble and then dissolve. in a strict canon, the copying continues throughout. josquin des prez makes these entries an audible means of articulating a text. in ave maria ... virgo serena, the opening greeting passes through successive voices before the texture changes. new clauses can receive new motifs, paired voices can answer other pairs, and all the singers can come together for a direct utterance. imitation draws its force from contrast with fewer parts, longer notes and coordinated syllables. ottaviano petrucci’s misse josquin of 1502 gave one composer’s masses a printed collection, helping the repertory circulate beyond the institutions that commissioned or copied it. giovanni pierluigi da palestrina’s roman church music controls dissonance through the motion of individual parts. a suspension begins as a consonant note, is held while another voice changes beneath it, then resolves down by step. passing notes usually occupy weaker positions. leaps are balanced by stepwise movement, and the lines avoid repeatedly reaching perfect consonances in parallel motion. later counterpoint teaching extracted a more regular classroom style from this varied musical practice. the legend of the rescuethe council of trent met between 1545 and 1563. its reforms concerned abuses in worship. the story that one performance of palestrina’s missa papae marcelli saved all polyphony from prohibition lacks contemporary evidence; giuseppe baini’s 1828 biography helped consolidate the legend. the missa papae marcelli, published in 1567, normally uses six voices and expands to seven in its final agnus dei. its gloria and credo often align the words across groups of singers, giving polyphony clear declamation. palestrina’s carefully prepared dissonances also make musical tension audible without requiring abrupt chromatic changes. to hear the mechanism, follow a single held note across the moment when the other voices move: the same pitch changes from stable to unstable before its own resolution. thomas tallis’s spem in alium, probably composed around 1570, uses forty separate parts arranged in eight five-part choirs. entries travel through successive groups, accumulate and give way to passages for the full ensemble. its original occasion and layout remain uncertain. the technical problem is concrete: maintaining independent lines while controlling when the listener hears one group, neighbouring groups or all forty voices. polyphony can organise physical separation as well as melodic agreement.

title: How did singing become a way to act?
k: how did singing become a way to act? the words take command before bach c. 1570–1607 in florence during the 1570s and 1580s, giovanni de’ bardi’s circle of musicians and scholars discussed how ancient greek drama had been performed. the group later called the camerata included vincenzo galilei, galileo’s father, and the singer-composer giulio caccini. their knowledge of ancient sound was fragmentary. what they could act on was an argument: a single voice, supported without competing words, could deliver a text more directly than several singers pursuing different phrases at once. monody means a solo vocal line with instrumental accompaniment. around 1600, an explicitly declamatory style over a written bass gave this longstanding practice new forms in print and on stage. caccini’s le nuove musiche, published in 1602, offered songs with instructions on delivery and ornament. jacopo peri’s largely lost dafne, performed in florence in 1598, and his surviving euridice of 1600 applied related ideas to continuous drama. recitative is composed speecha singer may repeat one pitch through several syllables, lengthen a stressed word and move at a cadence while the bass changes slowly. the rhythm follows dramatic syntax more closely than a dance, but the notes and bass still make a composed musical argument. the dispute over expressive dissonance developed partly within the older medium of the polyphonic madrigal. in publications of 1600 and 1603, giovanni maria artusi attacked passages from music by claudio monteverdi, initially without naming him. his examples included unprepared or unusually approached dissonances that violated the contrapuntal teaching artusi defended. removing the words from such examples made their intervals easy to inspect but excluded the evidence monteverdi considered decisive: the particular meaning and emphasis of the text. monteverdi’s fifth book of madrigals appeared in 1605 with cruda amarilli, one of the disputed works, and a brief response promising an account of his practice. in 1607 his brother giulio cesare’s explanation in the scherzi musicali distinguished the seconda pratica, in which the words govern the musical treatment, from the inherited prima pratica. monteverdi continued to compose in learned older styles, while allowing a poetic demand to justify a dissonance that a detached interval exercise would reject. a documented sequencethe publications, letters and performances behind the controversy are set out in the journal of seventeenth-century music chronology. the argument concerns madrigals before it becomes shorthand for the birth of opera. l’orfeo, with a libretto by alessandro striggio, was first performed at the gonzaga court in mantua on 24 february 1607. its five acts combine recitative, solo song, choruses, dances and instrumental ritornellos, making the contrast between musical types part of the drama. a shepherd’s measured song and the messenger’s report of eurydice’s death demand different kinds of delivery. in ‘tu se’ morta’, orpheus’s repeated questions and widening vocal gestures turn the news into a resolve to enter the underworld. the printed score of 1609 names a substantial instrumental collection, including strings, cornetts, trombones, harpsichords, organs, chitarroni and a double harp. the contrasting bass resources help distinguish pastoral scenes from the underworld. in ‘possente spirto’, orpheus attempts to persuade the ferryman through increasingly elaborate song, with instrumental responses between the vocal phrases. the score supplies both an ornamented vocal line and a plainer alternative. vocal display has a dramatic function: orpheus is a musician trying to make his art change another character’s decision. the courts supplied the earliest productions with money, performers and invited audiences. venice’s public opera theatres, beginning in 1637, later changed that institutional arrangement. by then monteverdi had served at san marco since 1613; the composer of courtly orfeo would also write for the city’s commercial stage. the new genre’s continuity lay in a practical division of labour: the singer delivers the words, the bass supports their pacing, and instruments can intervene when speech alone is no longer the scene’s only action.

title: How can a bass line guide everyone else?
sub: The bass becomes a working plan
k: how can a bass line guide everyone else? the bass becomes a working plan before bach c. 1600–1722 a continuo part gives an accompanist a bass line from which to build the harmony. figures specify intervals above that bass; the player supplies a suitable spacing, texture and voice-leading. a keyboard or plucked-string instrument can provide the harmony, often with a bowed bass instrument or bassoon reinforcing the written line. the combination varies with place, genre and available musicians. ‘continuo’ names the practice and its function across these different ensembles. some roots of the practice lie in organ accompaniment that followed the lowest sounding voice of a choral texture, the basso seguente. around 1600, an independent written bass became central to solo song, sacred concertos and theatre. lodovico da viadana’s cento concerti ecclesiastici of 1602, for small vocal forces with organ, helped disseminate the practice. a composer could now write a solo line against a continuous harmonic support, leaving the inner parts to the accompanist. read upwards from the bassa figure 6 normally asks for a sixth above the written note, with a third commonly understood. a bare sharp or flat commonly alters the third. the figures describe sounding intervals measured from the bass. with c in the bass, an unfigured consonant sonority will often contain e and g. with e in the bass and a 6, the player may supply g and c: the same c-major triad in another position. the bass note can therefore differ from the chord’s root. a 4–3 figure can require c to remain over a g bass before resolving down to b. that one suspension joins the older discipline of prepared dissonance to a notation designed for practical accompaniment. realisation still requires decisions about register, doubling, rhythm and the movement of each part. seventeenth-century music increasingly organises these sonorities around a tonic and cadences that confirm it. a bass moving from g to c, together with b rising to c in another voice, can establish c as a local centre. repeated cadential patterns, sequences and contrasting key areas gradually make major–minor tonality a stronger organising principle. modal habits, contrapuntal formulas and newer bass-led patterns coexist for decades. rameau’s traite de l’harmonie of 1722 later explains chords through roots and inversions, distinguishing a theoretical fundamental bass from the lowest notes actually played. the tuning compromisetwelve pure fifths differ from seven octaves. a tuning must distribute or isolate the discrepancy. changing the tuning changes the sizes of thirds and fifths while the written notes stay the same. quarter-comma meantone narrows the fifths so that several major thirds become pure 5:4 intervals. on a conventional twelve-note keyboard, however, the chain leaves a badly mistuned ‘wolf’ interval and makes some remote keys impractical. extra keys or split accidentals can provide alternatives, but require a different instrument. twelve-tone equal temperament instead divides the octave into twelve equal semitones. every key then has the same interval pattern: fifths are slightly narrow and major thirds appreciably wider than pure thirds. these adjustments allow unrestricted transposition. unequal circulating temperaments offer another solution: all keys remain usable, but their intervals differ. ‘well-tempered’ encompasses a wider range of tunings than ‘equal-tempered’. bach’s first book of the well-tempered clavier, dated 1722, contains a prelude and fugue in each of the twelve major and twelve minor keys. the title leaves the precise tuning open. the practical inheritance visible in those pieces includes far more than tuning: a fixed staff, measured durations, independent voices, recurring bass patterns and the ability to carry a musical argument through several keys.
